items.title: openstan — Free UK Bank Statement Analyser
items.text:
Parse, analyse, and export your UK bank statement PDFs in seconds. Free, open source, and 100% offline — your data never leaves your machine.

"I built openstan because I was manually typing HSBC statements into spreadsheets for my self-assessment tax return. There had to be a better way." — Jason Farrar, creator

Import an entire year of statements, build reports, and export to Excel in under a minute. No subscription. No account. No internet connection required. No Python or database knowledge needed.

items.title: What openstan does
items.text:
• Import bank statement PDFs from any supported bank — one file at a time or whole folders at once.
  • Review import results: successful statements are committed to your project database; statements that need attention are highlighted with full debug output and the original PDF side by side.
  • Summarise your project: transaction counts, account breakdowns, and automatic detection of statement coverage gaps (missing months flagged clearly).
  • Export to Excel, CSV, or JSON — either as a flat transactions table or a full star-schema dataset (accounts, calendar, statements, transactions, balances, gaps).
  • Build reports with a no-code report builder: filter, group, and aggregate your transactions, save named configurations, and export results.
  • Advanced export — spec-driven custom exports via TOML files with per-account and date-range filtering.
  • Anonymise bank statement PDFs for safe sharing with AI, accountants, or bug reports — all processing happens locally.

items.title: Privacy
items.text:
openstan makes one outbound network call: a silent version check on startup. No statement data, no telemetry, no analytics, no account registration. See the full Privacy Policy.

Your bank statements are sensitive. They stay on your machine.

items.title: Supported banks
items.text:
openstan parses statements using the bank_statement_parser library. The following banks and account types are currently supported:

Bank Supported account types Halifax Bank UK Current Account HSBC Bank UK Rewards Credit Card, Flexible Saver (Savings Account), Bank Account (Current Account), HSBC Advance (Current Account), Online Bonus Saver (Savings Account) NatWest Bank UK Select Account (Current Account) TSB Bank UK Spend & Save (Current Account)

New banks can be added by anyone via a TOML configuration file — no coding required. Don't see your bank? Request it here.

items.title: Contributing to Documentation
items.text: This guide covers standards and best practices for contributing to the openstan user guide. All documentation pages must follow these principles to maintain consistency, readability, and search engine visibility.

items.title: Quick Checklist
items.text:
Before submitting a documentation change, ensure:

  • [ ] Frontmatter includes a page-specific description field (150–160 characters)
  • [ ] description is unique and summarizes the page's value, not the site description
  • [ ] Page has a single H1 heading (the title)
  • [ ] Internal links use relative paths (e.g., [link](../guides/export-data.md))
  • [ ] All images have descriptive alt text and follow theme conventions (#only-light / #only-dark for theme-variant images)
  • [ ] Code examples are clear, tested, and include language hints (```python)
  • [ ] Page is linked from at least one related page (internal linking for crawlability)

items.title: Frontmatter Structure
items.text:
Every documentation page must include frontmatter with a description field:

---
description: "Import 12 months of bank statement PDFs, separate business from personal transactions, and export clean data for your Self Assessment tax return. 100% offline."
---

# Page Title

items.title: Description Field Requirements
items.text:
The description field is critical for SEO — it appears in: - Google Search results (SERP snippets) - Open Graph meta tags (social media previews) - Twitter Card summaries (Twitter/X)

Guidelines:

  • Length: 150–160 characters (Google shows 150–160 chars in search results)
  • Uniqueness: Must be specific to the page, not the generic site description
  • Search intent: Begin with action verbs or clear value propositions:
  • ✅ "Import 12 months of bank statement PDFs, separate business from personal..."
  • ✅ "Step-by-step guide to creating your first project, importing bank statements..."
  • ❌ "User guide for openstan — a desktop application..." (generic site description)
  • Keyword inclusion: Naturally include 1–2 target keywords (not stuffed):
  • ✅ "Export committed transaction data to Excel, CSV, or JSON..."
  • ❌ "Export export export to Excel CSV JSON..."
  • Avoid: Periods, promotional language ("Best!", "Amazing!"), or brand mentions unless necessary

Examples:

Page Good Description Why /installation/ "Install openstan on Windows, macOS, or Linux. Self-contained native installers — no Python required." Clear value prop, search-friendly keywords (install, platforms) /use-cases/self-assessment/ "Import 12 months of bank statement PDFs, separate business from personal transactions, and export clean data for your Self Assessment tax return. 100% offline." Action-focused, includes search intent (self-assessment, bank statements) /guides/export-data/ "Export committed transaction data from openstan to Excel, CSV, or JSON using configurable presets." Specific outcome, formats listed /quickstart/ "Step-by-step guide to creating your first project, importing bank statement PDFs, and exporting transactions in openstan." Begins with intent, covers workflow

items.title: Headings (H1, H2, H3)
items.text:
• H1 (one per page): Page title, always auto-generated from frontmatter or Markdown H1
  • H2 (sections): Major topic divisions
  • Nest logically; avoid skipping levels (H1 → H2 → H3, not H1 → H3)
  • Keep to 2–5 per page for readability
  • H3 (subsections): Detail within major sections
  • Use sparingly; too many indicates content should be split across pages

Example structure:

# Main Feature Title

## Overview / When to Use This

## Key Concepts or Prerequisites

### Sub-topic A

### Sub-topic B

## Step-by-Step Guide (if applicable)

## Common Issues & Troubleshooting

## Related Topics

items.title: Content Flow
items.text:
1. Opening paragraph (2–3 sentences):
  2. Restate what the page is about (users skim)
  3. Mention search keywords naturally

  4. Link to related pages if needed

  5. Body sections:

  6. Use H2 for major topics
  7. Start sections with brief intent statements

  8. Include examples, screenshots, or code where helpful

  9. Closing:

  10. Optional: "See Also" or "Related Topics" section with 3–5 internal links
  11. Links must use relative paths and point to .md files (MkDocs converts to URLs)

items.title: Internal Linking
items.text: Internal links help Google crawl and understand your site structure. They also improve user navigation.

items.title: Guidelines
items.text:
• Link frequently (3–5 links per ~1,000 words is typical)
  • Use descriptive anchor text: ❌ "Click here" → ✅ "Export Data" or "See the export guide"
  • Link to related pages:
  • Use-case pages should link to relevant screen/feature pages
  • Screen pages should link back to use cases that use them
  • Sequential guides should link forward/backward
  • Use relative paths: [Export Data](../guides/export-data.md) — MkDocs converts to URLs automatically
  • Avoid linking to the same page (e.g., don't link to /guides/export-data/ from within that same page)

Example — Page Linking Map:

/use-cases/self-assessment/
├─ Links to: /guides/export-data/ (to export for tax)
├─ Links to: /guides/run-reports/ (to build custom reports)
├─ Links to: ../index.md (back to all use cases)
└─ Links to: ../installation.md (getting started)

items.title: Best Practices
items.text:
• Alt text: Every image must have descriptive alt text (![description](path))
  • ✅ "Project Management panel showing statement queue with 3 PDFs"

  • ❌ "screenshot" or leaving empty

  • Theme variants: For light/dark theme screenshots, use fragment identifiers: 

    ![Alt text — light](assets/screenshots/foo.png#only-light)
![Alt text — dark](assets/screenshots/dark/foo.png#only-dark)

  • Light variants go in assets/screenshots/
  • Dark variants go in assets/screenshots/dark/

  • Zensical CSS hides the non-matching variant per user's theme

  • File size: Optimize images before committing (compression, reasonable dimensions)

items.title: Code Examples
items.text:
• Use language-specific code blocks: 
    # Good
def my_function():
    pass

# Avoid (no language hint)
def my_function():
  • Testability: Examples should be runnable (or clearly show what a user would do)
  • Comments: Use inline comments to explain non-obvious logic
  • Syntax highlighting: Ensure the language is specified for proper highlighting

items.title: Tone
items.text:
• Clear, direct, and helpful
  • Avoid jargon; explain technical terms on first use
  • Write for UK English (e.g., "analyse" not "analyze")

items.title: Common Patterns
items.text:
• Instructional: "To import statements, click Import (Ctrl+I)..."
  • Conceptual: "The Export Data panel separates committed transactions from queued imports..."
  • Cautionary: "⚠️ Deleting a project cannot be undone."

items.title: Formatting
items.text:
• Bold for UI buttons/menu items: "Click File → Export"
  • Code font for file paths, commands, config keys: project.db, uv run openstan
  • Monospace blocks for terminal output or structured data
  • Admonitions (if supported) for notes/warnings: 
    !!! note "Important"
    This is a note.

!!! warning "Be careful"
    This is a warning.

items.title: Code Signing Policy
items.text:
openstan installers are code-signed to verify authenticity and integrity.

  • Windows: signed with a Certum Open Source Code Signing certificate using jsign.
  • macOS: signed with an Apple Developer ID Application certificate, notarized by Apple, and stapled.

items.title: Windows
items.text:
Windows installers (.msi) for openstan are code-signed using a certificate issued to Open Source Developer Jason Telford Farrar by Certum Code Signing 2021 CA (Asseco Data Systems S.A.).

The certificate is an OV (Organisation Validation) Open Source Code Signing certificate stored in Certum's SimplySign cloud-based virtual smartcard.

The signature covers the MSI installer package. It confirms that the installer was produced by an automated, verifiable build from the source code in this repository.

items.title: macOS
items.text:
macOS builds (.app inside .dmg) are signed with an Apple Developer ID Application certificate. The signed app is submitted to Apple's notarisation service, and the notarisation ticket is stapled to the bundle before the DMG is created.

This means Gatekeeper will trust the application on double-click — no right-click workaround is required.

items.title: Team roles
items.text:

openstan does not collect personal data. The only outbound network request is a silent update check on startup (HTTPS to api.github.com; no personal data transmitted). Users can disable this in the application settings.

items.title: Build and release process
items.text:
1. A version tag (e.g. v1.0.0) is pushed to the GitHub repository.
  2. The GitHub Actions release workflow runs automatically:
  3. Dependencies are installed via uv sync
  4. The application is frozen with cx_Freeze

items.title: Windows
items.text:
• The MSI installer is compiled with WiX v4
  • The unsigned MSI is attached to the GitHub Release as a draft
  • The maintainer manually signs the MSI using jsign + SimplySign Desktop:
  • Authenticate SimplySign Desktop (requires OTP from Android app)
  • Run jsign --storetype PKCS11 --keystore ~/provider_simplysign.cfg ...
  • Re-upload the signed MSI to the draft release
  • The signed MSI is verified, then the draft release is promoted to published.

items.title: macOS
items.text:
• The .app bundle is signed with codesign (Developer ID, hardened runtime)
  • The signed .app is submitted to Apple's notary service via notarytool
  • The notarisation ticket is stapled with xcrun stapler
  • The DMG is created and signed separately

All build configuration is in the public repository. The release workflow and WiX installer source (packaging/windows/openstan.wxs) are open to inspection.

items.text: If you believe a signed openstan installer contains malware or has been signed with a compromised certificate, please report it to Certum support and open an issue on the openstan issue tracker.

items.title: Windows
items.text:
1. Download the .msi installer from the latest release.
  2. Double-click the .msi file to launch the installer.
  3. Follow the on-screen prompts. openstan is installed per-user by default (no administrator rights needed).
  4. Launch openstan from the Start menu or desktop shortcut.

Windows SmartScreen

Windows installers are code-signed via Certum Open Source Code Signing certificate. SmartScreen may still show a warning on first run for newly signed applications. Click More info → Run anyway to proceed. See the Code signing policy for details.

items.title: macOS
items.text:
1. Download the .dmg disk image from the latest release.
  2. Open the .dmg and drag openstan into your Applications folder.
  3. Double-click to launch openstan. The app is signed and notarized by Apple, so Gatekeeper will trust it automatically.

Gatekeeper

openstan macOS builds are signed with an Apple Developer ID certificate and notarized by Apple. You can launch the app normally — no right-click workaround is required. See the Code signing policy for details.

items.title: Linux (Debian / Ubuntu)
items.text:
Download the .deb package from the latest release matching your system architecture (x86_64 or ARM64) and install it:

sudo apt install ./openstan-*.deb

After installation, launch openstan from your application menu, or run openstan in a terminal.

Both x86_64 and ARM64 packages are available.

items.title: Dependencies installed automatically
items.text: The .deb package declares libxcb-cursor0 as a runtime dependency; apt will install it automatically. All other libraries (Qt, Python, OpenSSL, etc.) are bundled inside the installer.

sudo dnf install ./openstan-*.rpm

items.title: Summary
items.text: openstan does not collect, transmit, or store any personal data outside your own machine. No account is required and no internet connection is needed to use the application.

items.title: Data storage
items.text: All data created by openstan — including imported bank statements, parsed transactions, project configuration, and exported files — is written exclusively to folders on your own device. You choose where each project folder is created. openstan has no servers and no cloud storage. Your financial data never leaves your machine.

items.title: Network activity
items.text:
openstan makes one outbound network request: an update check on startup.

When the application launches, it silently queries the GitHub Releases API to compare the installed version against the latest published release. If a newer version is available, a dialog is shown offering a link to the release notes.

The request:

  • Is made over HTTPS to api.github.com
  • Sends only a standard HTTP User-Agent: openstan header
  • Does not transmit any personal data, usage data, or information about your project files
  • Fails silently if the network is unavailable — no error is shown and the application continues normally
  • Does not download or install anything automatically; downloading an update is always a manual action by the user

No other network requests are made by openstan.

items.title: Optional exchange rate data
items.text:
openstan may in a future release offer an opt-in feature to retrieve currency exchange rates from a third-party API. This feature:

  • Is strictly optional and disabled by default — it will only make network requests if you explicitly enable it
  • Will send only the currency codes required to fetch a rate (e.g. GBP, USD) — no personal data, transaction amounts, or account details are transmitted
  • Will be clearly labelled in the application settings with a description of what data is sent and to which service

This section will be updated with the specific API provider and its privacy policy when the feature is released.

items.title: Telemetry and analytics
items.text: openstan contains no telemetry, crash reporting, usage analytics, or any other background data collection.

items.title: Third-party components
items.text: openstan uses open-source libraries (PySide6, Polars, and others) as listed in the project's pyproject.toml. None of these libraries are configured to collect or transmit data in the context of openstan.

items.title: Code signing
items.text: Platform installers are code-signed to verify authenticity and integrity. Windows installers are signed via Certum Open Source Code Signing. macOS builds are signed with an Apple Developer ID certificate and notarized by Apple. The signing process does not involve any user data.

items.title: Quick Start
items.text: This guide walks you through the full workflow from a fresh installation to your first committed batch of statements.

items.title: Video walkthrough
items.text:
Prefer watching? These videos walk through the same steps covered below.

Quick overview (2 min) — import, review, commit.

Full walkthrough (12 min) — includes reports, advanced export, and tips.

items.title: Step 1 — Launch openstan
items.text: Open openstan from your application menu or desktop shortcut. On first run you will see a welcome screen with options to create a new project or add an existing one.

items.title: Step 2 — Create a project
items.text:
A project is a folder on disk that holds your statement PDFs, configuration files, and the parsed transaction database. Each project is self-contained and portable.

  1. Click Create New Project in the project selector bar.
  2. Enter a Project Name (e.g. Personal Finances).
  3. Click Choose Folder and select the parent directory where you want the project folder to be created. openstan will create a subfolder with the project name inside the directory you choose.
  4. Click Finish.

The new project is selected automatically and the project selector bar appears.

Adding an existing project

If you have already created a project on another machine or moved a project folder, use Add Existing Project instead. Navigate to the existing project folder and openstan will register it in the UI without changing any files.

items.title: Step 3 — Add statements to the import queue
items.text:
1. Click Import Statements in the navigation bar (or press Alt+I).
  2. Use Add Folders of Statements to add a whole directory of PDFs at once, or Add Individual Statement Files to pick specific files. Files are shown in a tree grouped by folder.
  3. Review the queue. Use Remove Selected or Clear All Statements to adjust the list.

items.title: Step 4 — Run the import
items.text:
Click Run Statement Import. openstan sends each PDF to the parser in the background. A progress bar shows the overall status.

When processing is complete, the results panel opens automatically.

items.title: Step 5 — Review results
items.text:
The results panel shows three tabs:

Tab Meaning SUCCESS Statements parsed cleanly — these can be committed. REVIEW Statements parsed but the checks-and-balances totals do not match. FAILURE Statements that could not be parsed at all.

For REVIEW and FAILURE rows, click View Debug Info to open a dialog with per-file debug output and the original PDF side by side.

Unsupported banks

If all your statements appear in the FAILURE tab, your bank may not yet have a parser configuration. See the bank_statement_parser guide on adding a new bank for instructions on creating a TOML config file.

items.title: Step 6 — Commit the batch
items.text:
When you are satisfied with the results, click Commit Batch. Only SUCCESS-status statements are written to the project database. REVIEW and FAILURE statements remain unimported.

Once committed, the queue unlocks and the Project Info, Export Data, and Run Reports navigation items become visible.

items.title: Step 7 — Explore your data
items.text:
• Project Info (Alt+P) — summary statistics, per-account breakdowns, and any coverage gaps detected between consecutive statements.
  • Export Data (Alt+E) — export transactions to Excel, CSV, or JSON.
  • Run Reports (Alt+R) — build custom reports with filters, grouping, and aggregations, and export or preview them live.

items.title: Next steps
items.text:
• Read the Import Statements screen guide for full details on the queue and import options.
  • Read the Export Data and Advanced Export guides to learn about export specs.
  • Read the Run Reports guide to get the most out of the report builder.
  • If an import fails, enable verbose mode and check the Project Log — see the Logging & Debugging Guide for instructions.

items.title: Troubleshooting
items.text: Need help? This guide covers common issues and solutions.

items.title: "The import fails or shows errors"
items.text:
Check the Import Results screen:

  1. After import completes, click View Results or go to the Import Results screen
  2. Look for the Issue Summary section
  3. Check which fields/banks failed

For detailed diagnostics:

  1. Enable verbose mode: Admin → Logging Settings → Check "Enable verbose mode"
  2. Try the import again
  3. Click Admin → View Project Log
  4. Look for error messages in the log
  5. Disable verbose mode when done

Common issues:

Issue Solution "Unrecognized bank format" The PDF format isn't supported for this bank yet. Check bank_statement_parser issues for status. "Could not extract field X" The field exists in the PDF but parser couldn't read it. Enable verbose mode for details. File an issue with the PDF (redacted). "PDF is corrupted or password-protected" Try opening the PDF in your PDF reader to confirm it's valid. Password-protected files aren't supported. "Out of memory" You're importing too many statements at once. Split into smaller batches.

items.title: "Statement imports are very slow"
items.text:
Normal behavior: Importing 10–20 statements takes 2–5 minutes depending on size and complexity.

If it's taking longer than expected:

  1. Check your system resources (open System Monitor/Task Manager)
  2. Close other applications consuming CPU/memory
  3. Enable verbose mode and check logs for per-field extraction timing
  4. Try importing a smaller batch

items.title: "I don't see logs in the viewer"
items.text:
Possible causes:

  1. Log file doesn't exist yet
  2. App has just started; perform an action (import, export) to generate entries
  3. Click Refresh button in the log viewer

  4. Solution: Perform an operation, then check logs again

  5. Wrong log selected

  6. App Log is always available
  7. Project Log only appears when a project is selected

  8. Solution: Make sure you've selected a project

  9. File permissions issue

  10. App doesn't have write access to log directory
  11. Solution (Linux): Check chmod on ~/.local/share/openstan/ (should be user-owned)

  12. Solution (Windows/macOS): Try opening log file manually (see Finding Log Files Manually)

  13. Enable verbose mode for more output

  14. Normal log level only shows milestones and errors
  15. DEBUG level shows many more entries
  16. Solution: Admin → Logging Settings → Check "Enable verbose mode"

items.title: "Logs are growing too large"
items.text:
Normal behavior: Logs rotate automatically at 10 MB and keep 5 backups (~60 MB total).

To reduce output:

  • Disable verbose mode: Admin → Logging Settings → Uncheck "Enable verbose mode"
  • Logs won't shrink until files rotate, but new logging will be quieter

Manual cleanup (if disk space is critical):

  1. Navigate to log directory (see Finding Log Files Manually)
  2. Delete old session files (safe; each file is one session)
  3. Keep current session's log file (app still writing to it)

Linux example: 

cd ~/.local/share/openstan/
# List files by date (newest first)
ls -lt
# Delete old sessions (more than 30 days old)
find . -name "*.log*" -mtime +30 -delete

items.title: "Verbose mode is showing too much output"
items.text:
Expected behavior: Verbose mode increases output 3–5× compared to normal.

DEBUG logging shows:

  • Per-field extraction details (slow fields identified)
  • Database operations (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE)
  • Library diagnostics from bank_statement_parser and uk_bank_statement_anonymiser

Solution:

  • Disable verbose mode when done troubleshooting
  • Admin → Logging Settings → Uncheck "Enable verbose mode"
  • Changes apply immediately (no restart needed)

items.title: "How do I share logs with support?"
items.text:
Step 1: Enable verbose mode (optional, for detailed info) - Admin → Logging Settings → Check "Enable verbose mode" - Perform the action that's failing - Wait 10–30 seconds

Step 2: Gather logs - Admin → View App Log or View Project Log - Click Copy button

Step 3: Redact sensitive data - Review logs and remove account numbers, names, etc. (use **** as placeholder) - See Sharing Logs with Support for examples

Step 4: Submit - GitHub issue - Or community@openstan.org

items.title: "Export fails or produces unexpected output"
items.text:
Check the export settings:

  1. Go to Export Data screen (Alt+E)
  2. Verify:
  3. Export Type is correct (Single/Split/Pivot)
  4. Output Format is correct (Excel/CSV/JSON)
  5. Date range and filters are correct
  6. Try exporting a smaller date range

For diagnostics:

  1. Enable verbose mode: Admin → Logging Settings → Check "Enable verbose mode"
  2. Perform the export
  3. View Project Log and look for error messages
  4. Disable verbose mode when done

items.title: "The Excel file is corrupted"
items.text:
Possible causes:

  1. Antivirus software blocked the file — Check your antivirus logs
  2. File was partially written — Not enough disk space available
  3. File is too large — Excel has a 1M row limit; use CSV for very large datasets

Solutions:

  • Check your free disk space
  • Try exporting to CSV instead
  • Split the export into smaller date ranges
  • Disable antivirus temporarily (only for testing)

items.title: "Export is very slow"
items.text:
Normal behavior: Exporting 100k+ rows takes 1–2 minutes depending on export type.

To speed up:

  • Export smaller date range
  • Use "Single" export type (faster than Split or Pivot)
  • Close other applications
  • Check disk space (slow disk = slow export)

items.title: "Anonymisation fails or takes too long"
items.text:
First check:

  1. Enable verbose mode: Admin → Logging Settings → Check "Enable verbose mode"
  2. Try anonymising a single statement first
  3. View Project Log and look for errors
  4. Check the anonymisation results screen

Common issues:

Issue Solution "PDF is corrupted or password-protected" Try opening in PDF reader first. Anonymiser doesn't support password-protected PDFs. "Exclusion patterns didn't match" Check regex patterns are correct. Test with a simple pattern first. "Anonymisation is very slow" Large PDFs (100+ pages) can take 30+ seconds. Normal behavior. "Output PDF is corrupted" Try anonymising a different statement first. File an issue with the PDF (redacted).

items.title: "Can't find the anonymised PDFs"
items.text:
Default location: Same folder as the source PDF files

To check:

  1. In Import Statements, find the folder you imported from
  2. Look for a _anonymised/ subfolder in that directory
  3. Files are named: [original-name]_anonymised.pdf

If not found:

  1. Check the anonymisation results screen
  2. Enable verbose mode and try again
  3. Look in Project Log for file path information

items.title: "App won't start or crashes on startup"
items.text:
Check the App Log:

  1. Navigate to log directory manually (see Finding Log Files Manually)
  2. Open the most recent log file with a text editor
  3. Look for ERROR messages at the end

Common startup issues:

Platform Issue Solution Windows "Missing library" error Reinstall the app (may be incomplete installation). Try latest installer macOS "App is damaged" warning App wasn't downloaded properly. Re-download and try again. Linux Qt library errors Install Qt dependencies. See Installation Guide

To debug further:

  1. Enable verbose mode: Create a new project and check logs
  2. Try running from a different location (e.g., USB drive)
  3. Check for recently installed security software blocking the app
  4. Report issue with App Log attached (see Sharing Logs with Support)

items.title: "Database error: 'gui.db' is locked or corrupted"
items.text:
The database is locked:

  1. Close all openstan windows
  2. Wait 30 seconds
  3. Restart the app

The database is corrupted:

  1. Backup your projects: ~/.local/share/openstan/projects/ (Linux example)
  2. Delete ~/.local/share/openstan/gui.db
  3. Restart the app (creates new empty database)
  4. Try re-opening your projects

If issue persists:

  • Report with App Log attached
  • Include your platform and app version (Help → About)

items.title: "I've followed all steps and still have issues"
items.text:
Collect logs:

  1. Enable verbose mode: Admin → Logging Settings
  2. Reproduce the issue
  3. Gather both App Log and Project Log (if applicable)

Report the issue:

  1. GitHub issue
  2. Include:
  3. Description of what you did
  4. What error you saw
  5. Your platform (Windows/macOS/Linux)
  6. App version (Help → About)

  7. Relevant log excerpts (with PII redacted)

  8. Or email: community@openstan.org

items.title: How to Redact or Anonymise a Bank Statement (Free, Step-by-Step)
items.text:
You need to share your bank statements — with a mortgage lender, a solicitor, or your accountant. But handing over a full statement means exposing your account number, sort code, and every personal transaction note to someone who only needs to verify your balance.

The question isn't whether to redact. It's how much you can remove before the document becomes unverifiable — and what happens if you get that wrong.
path: How to Redact or Anonymise a Bank Statement (Free, Step-by-Step)

items.title: How to Redact or Anonymise a Bank Statement (Free, Step-by-Step)
items.text: This guide covers exactly what to remove, what you must keep, and how to do it consistently using openstan — a free tool that processes your statements locally, so nothing is uploaded to any server.
path: How to Redact or Anonymise a Bank Statement (Free, Step-by-Step)

items.title: When you might need to anonymise a bank statement
items.text:
Before getting into the how, it helps to be clear about the situation you're in — because the answer to "how much can I redact?" depends partly on who is receiving the document and why.

Common scenarios:

  • Mortgage application: Your lender needs to see income deposits and spending patterns. They do not need your full account number, sort code, or personal transaction notes.
  • Probate / estate administration: You're sharing statements with a solicitor who needs to establish the value of an estate. They need balances and transaction totals, not personal identifiers.
  • Accountant or tax preparer: They need to see amounts and dates for reconciliation. Personal memos, payee names for private transactions, and account details are rarely relevant.
  • Court proceedings (e.g. child support, financial disclosure): Proof of funds is required, but you may wish to limit unnecessary personal exposure.
  • Landlord reference: Showing proof of regular income without revealing everything else in your account.

One scenario worth noting separately: if you're sharing statements with an agent acting on your behalf for HMRC self-assessment, the agent typically needs originals — HMRC requires complete records. For guidance on what HMRC specifically needs, see HMRC Bank Statements for Self-Assessment.

A growing concern with any professional sharing is that third parties may feed your documents into AI tools — ChatGPT, Copilot, or similar — to summarise or analyse them. An unredacted bank statement sent to an AI assistant exposes your account number, sort code, and full transaction history to external servers. Anonymising before you share means that risk disappears regardless of what the recipient does with the file.
path: How to Redact or Anonymise a Bank Statement (Free, Step-by-Step)

items.title: What to remove
items.text:
These are the fields you can safely redact without affecting the document's usefulness for verification purposes.

  • ❌ Full account holder name — once you've provided identity separately (e.g. a copy of your passport), the name on the statement is redundant
  • ❌ Full account number — redact to the last 4 digits only; this is enough for the recipient to confirm which account they're looking at
  • ❌ Sort code — not required to verify balances or transaction history
  • ❌ Bank branch address — too granular; the bank name is sufficient
  • ❌ Personal transaction memos — notes you've added yourself (e.g. "Dad's birthday", "holiday spending") have no verification value
  • ❌ Sensitive payee names — optional and case-by-case; if certain payees are private (medical, legal, personal), you can redact those specific rows

The key principle: remove anything that identifies you personally beyond what is strictly necessary for the recipient's purpose.
path: How to Redact or Anonymise a Bank Statement (Free, Step-by-Step)

items.title: What you must keep
items.text:
This is the part that generic redaction guides miss entirely. Removing too much makes the document useless — or worse, makes it look tampered with.

  • ✓ Transaction date — required to establish the period the statement covers
  • ✓ Transaction amount (debit and credit separately) — the core verification data
  • ✓ Running balance — this is the most important field to preserve; recipients use it to confirm the statement hasn't been altered, because a genuine statement will always show consistent arithmetic between each row
  • ✓ Bank name and logo — establishes where the document came from
  • ✓ Account type (Current / Savings) — provides context for the balance figures
  • ✓ Statement period (e.g. "1 October – 31 October 2025") — required for date range verification
  • ✓ Opening and closing balance — always keep these; they're the first thing a lender or solicitor will check

If the running balance column is missing from your anonymised version, expect the document to be rejected or questioned.
path: How to Redact or Anonymise a Bank Statement (Free, Step-by-Step)

items.title: Comparing your options
items.text:
There are several ways to redact a bank statement PDF. They differ significantly in how consistent they are, how private they are, and how much effort they require.

Method Effort Consistency Privacy risk Cost Manual — PDF editor (Adobe, Preview) High Low — easy to miss a field Low — local Free / paid Print, black pen, rescan Very high Very low — error-prone Low — local Free Online tool (Smallpdf, iLovePDF, Adobe online) Medium Medium High — statement uploaded to third-party server Free tier / paid openstan built-in anonymisation Low High — rule-based, applies consistently Low — local, nothing uploaded Free

The privacy risk of online tools deserves a specific note. When you upload a bank statement to Smallpdf, iLovePDF, or Adobe's online service, your document — including account numbers, sort codes, and full transaction history — is transmitted to and processed on their servers. For a document this sensitive, that is a meaningful risk. openstan runs entirely on your own computer. Your statements never leave your machine.
path: How to Redact or Anonymise a Bank Statement (Free, Step-by-Step)

items.title: Step-by-step: anonymise with openstan
items.text:
openstan is a free desktop tool for reading and exporting bank statement PDFs. The anonymisation feature works directly on your original PDFs — you don't need to import a statement first. If you haven't installed it yet, the installation guide takes about five minutes.

Step 1: Open the Anonymise tool

Click Anonymise Statements in the nav bar (or press Alt+A). The tool opens as a standalone dialog — no project import required.

Step 2: Select your PDF

Click Browse… to select a single statement, or Browse Folder… to process an entire folder at once. Folder mode is useful if you're preparing several months of statements for a mortgage application or probate — openstan processes each one and collects the output in a single anonymised/ subfolder.

Step 3: Run it first, then review

Before adjusting any settings, click Run Anonymisation straight away. openstan ships with its own built-in anonymisation rules that handle the most common bank statement patterns — sort codes, account numbers, card numbers, and similar structured data are replaced automatically.

When the run completes, click Open Original PDF and Open Anonymised PDF to view both side by side. Go through every page of the anonymised version and ask:

  • Is anything still visible that shouldn't be? → you'll add it to the Always Anonymise table
  • Is any structural text (column headers, balance labels) now unreadable? → you'll add it to the Never Anonymise table

For many statements, the built-in rules are sufficient and no further configuration is needed.

Step 4: Adjust if needed

If the first run flagged issues, use the two tabs to tune the output:

The Always Anonymise tab adds explicit string replacements that run before scrambling. Use it for anything the built-in rules missed — a name, a specific reference, or a branch address that appeared in the output:

Original Text Replacement Jane Smith Account Holder 11-22-33 00-00-00 12345678 00000000

The Never Anonymise tab protects structural text from being scrambled — column headers, balance labels, statement period text — so the document stays readable:

Phrase Balance Brought Forward Date Money In Money Out

Click Run Anonymisation again, compare both versions once more, and repeat until the output is right. Your changes are saved automatically per project.

What to think about for your recipient:

Before finalising, consider what the recipient actually needs to see — and what they don't. The right level of anonymisation varies: a lender may need your name visible to match the statement to your identity, but has no need for your sort code. An accountant may need transaction descriptions but not your account number. A solicitor may need balances and totals but nothing else.

If you're unsure, ask the recipient before you anonymise rather than after. It's easier to share a less-redacted version once than to go back and redo it.

One consideration worth raising: some professionals use AI tools to review or summarise documents. An unredacted bank statement fed into a general-purpose AI assistant exposes your account details, sort code, and full transaction history to third-party servers you have no visibility over. Anonymising before sharing — even with a trusted professional — removes that risk entirely. See Sharing with AI for more on this.

Step 5: File the output correctly

Output is saved automatically alongside your originals: single-file mode writes anonymised_[original filename].pdf next to the source; folder mode writes everything into an anonymised/ subfolder inside the folder you selected.

Keep the originals exactly where they are. Do not delete them. HMRC, a court, or a future audit may require the unredacted version, and once you've shared the anonymised copy there is no way to undo that.

For the full reference — including the Retain Descriptions option and config file locations — see the Anonymise PDFs guide.
path: How to Redact or Anonymise a Bank Statement (Free, Step-by-Step)

items.title: If you're doing it manually
items.text:
If you prefer not to use openstan, or you only have a single statement to deal with, here are the manual options — with their caveats.

Adobe Acrobat Pro (desktop): Use the dedicated Redact tool, not the annotation layer. Drawing a black rectangle over text in Acrobat does not remove the text — it merely covers it, and the underlying data is still present in the file. The Redact tool permanently deletes the content. After applying redactions, use "Apply All Redactions" before saving.

macOS Preview: The markup tool in Preview is annotation-only. Black shapes drawn over text can be removed or the text searched underneath them. This is not secure redaction. Do not use Preview for anything you intend to share securely.

Print, black pen, rescan: Genuinely removes the information, but results in a lower-quality document and is impractical for multi-page statements. The quality loss can itself raise questions.

After any manual redaction method, test it: open the resulting PDF, press Ctrl+F or Cmd+F, and search for your account number. If it appears in the search results, your redaction has not worked.
path: How to Redact or Anonymise a Bank Statement (Free, Step-by-Step)

items.title: Before you send
items.text:
A few checks worth doing regardless of which method you used:

  1. Read the anonymised version in full — don't assume the tool got everything; scroll every page
  2. Keep the original safe — store it separately and don't share the location
  3. Ask the recipient what they actually need — some mortgage underwriters require unredacted originals; a quick email saves you from having to redo this
  4. Password-protect the export — if you're sending by email, add a PDF password as an additional layer; share the password separately
  5. Confirm receipt — ask the recipient to acknowledge the file arrived and is readable
path: How to Redact or Anonymise a Bank Statement (Free, Step-by-Step)

items.title: FAQ
items.text:
Can I control exactly what gets anonymised? Yes. The Always Anonymise tab lets you specify exact strings to replace with safe placeholders (e.g. your sort code → 00-00-00). The Never Anonymise tab protects structural text from being scrambled. Everything else is scrambled by default — which is the safest starting point for sharing externally.

Is the anonymisation permanent? The anonymised output file has its text scrambled and specific values replaced — openstan does not store your original statements, and nothing is uploaded anywhere. The original PDF on your computer is untouched. Always keep that original; once you've shared the anonymised copy, you cannot un-share it.

Will a redacted statement be accepted by my mortgage lender? Most lenders accept redacted PDFs provided the transactions, dates, and running balance are all visible. Some underwriters require originals — it varies by lender and by the stage of the application. Check before you redact, not after.

What about CSV or Excel exports? This guide covers PDF statements. For CSV or Excel, simply delete the column containing the account number or name before sharing — no special tool needed. Be aware that spreadsheet metadata (document author, edit history) may also contain personal data; check the file properties before sending.

Does the bank name need to stay visible? Yes. The bank name establishes where the document came from. If a recipient can't tell which institution issued the statement, they have no basis to trust it. Do not remove the bank name or logo.

Can a redacted PDF be challenged in court? If redaction is done correctly — meaning the underlying data is permanently removed, not just covered — the document should not reveal the hidden information. Legal challenges to redaction typically focus on whether the right information was redacted, not on technical recovery. Using a proper redaction tool (not annotation) is important if the document may be used in legal proceedings.

items.text:
The self-assessment deadline is 31 January. Most people leave their bank statements until the last few weeks — and many discover too late that what they have isn't quite what HMRC expects.

The confusion is understandable: HMRC doesn't publish a precise checklist of formats and requirements. This guide fills that gap — what you need, what to avoid, how to check for gaps, and how long to keep everything.
path: HMRC Bank Statements for Self-Assessment: Complete Guide

items.title: What HMRC actually requires
items.text:
HMRC's guidance for self-employed taxpayers is set out on GOV.UK. According to that guidance, you must keep records of all your business income and expenses, and you must be able to "identify business transactions." Bank statements and chequebook stubs are listed explicitly as proof.

In practice, this means:

The right period. The UK tax year runs from 6 April to 5 April — not January to December. If you prepare twelve months of January-to-December statements, you're covering the wrong window. You need statements from 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026 for the 2025–26 tax year. Some sole traders use an accounting period that ends on a different date; if so, use that period consistently and note that you may need to allocate profits across two tax years.

Individual transactions, not summaries. GOV.UK requires that your records allow you to identify each business transaction. A monthly summary showing only a closing balance does not allow this. Download full statements that show every transaction, not an account overview page.

All relevant accounts. If income flows into your personal current account, that account is relevant. If you pay business expenses from a savings account, that one is too. There is no requirement to merge accounts — you can provide separate statements for each — but you need to include all of them.

Official downloads, not screenshots. GOV.UK does not specify a file format, but downloading statements from your bank's official portal (rather than screenshotting your banking app) gives you documents that clearly show the bank's header, account details, and statement period. These are more straightforwardly verifiable if HMRC ever asks to see them. Screenshots can be questioned.

A note on accounting method. From the 2024–25 tax year, cash basis is the default accounting method for self-employed taxpayers. Under cash basis, you record income and expenses when money is actually received or paid — which is what bank statements naturally reflect. If you've opted out of cash basis and use traditional accounting, your record-keeping requirements are more extensive: you'll also need records of amounts owed but not yet received, and committed but unpaid expenses.

You do not send statements with your tax return. GOV.UK states this explicitly: "You do not need to send your records in when you submit your tax return." You keep them and show them to HMRC if asked.

items.title: Common mistakes
items.text:
These are the ones that cause problems if HMRC requests your records:

  • ❌ Incomplete statements — downloading page 1 of a 6-page statement, or missing the final page where the closing balance appears
  • ❌ Summary view instead of full transactions — many banking apps show a monthly total rather than individual rows; the full statement is what you need
  • ❌ Wrong date range — January–December instead of April–April, or missing the final few days of March
  • ❌ Missing a secondary account — a PayPal account used for business, a savings account where invoices land, a second current account
  • ❌ Gaps between months — statements end on different days; make sure the closing balance of one month matches the opening balance of the next
  • ❌ Screenshots in place of downloaded statements — screenshots can be questioned as they don't carry the bank's official document structure

items.title: Step-by-step: preparing your statements

items.title: Step 1 — Identify all relevant accounts
items.text:
List every account where business income arrives or business expenses leave. This usually includes your main current account and may include savings accounts, a business account, or payment processor accounts like PayPal or Stripe.

If you're unsure whether a particular account is relevant, include it. It's easier to have more than you need than to go back for more later.
path: HMRC Bank Statements for Self-Assessment: Complete Guide

items.title: Step 2 — Download the right period
items.text:
Log in to each bank's online portal and download statements covering 6 April to 5 April. Most banks offer downloads by month or by statement period — download each one in turn.

A few practical notes:

  • Banks vary in how long they retain online statements — check your bank's own terms rather than assuming a specific number of years. If you need older statements, contact your bank sooner rather than later.
  • If your bank's portal only offers CSV or Excel downloads, request the PDF statements specifically — some banks keep them separately under a "documents" or "statements" section rather than the main account view.
  • Download to a dedicated folder named for the tax year, e.g. Self-Assessment-2025-26/HSBC/.
path: HMRC Bank Statements for Self-Assessment: Complete Guide

items.title: Step 3 — Check for gaps
items.text:
Lay your statements out in order and verify there are no missing months. Check that the closing balance on one statement matches the opening balance on the next — any discrepancy means either a missing statement or an overlapping download.

If you have multiple accounts, openstan can automate this: import your PDFs and the gap detection feature flags any missing periods across all accounts at once, so you don't have to check each one manually.

At the time of writing openstan supports Halifax, HSBC, NatWest, and TSB — see the full supported banks list. If your bank isn't listed, you can request it or add it yourself via a TOML configuration file — no coding required.
path: HMRC Bank Statements for Self-Assessment: Complete Guide

items.title: Step 4 — Verify each statement is complete
items.text:
Before filing anything away, spot-check each PDF:

  • Does it show individual transactions or just a summary?
  • Is the bank's official header present with the account name, sort code, and statement period?
  • Is the closing balance on the last page? (It's easy to download an incomplete statement if your bank paginates differently from what you expect.)
path: HMRC Bank Statements for Self-Assessment: Complete Guide

items.title: Step 5 — Decide on sharing format
items.text:
If you're working with an accountant, they may want the statements in spreadsheet form for easier filtering. openstan can export all your statements to a single Excel or CSV file — see the Export Data guide for options.

If you're sharing the PDFs directly, consider anonymising them first. Bank statements contain account numbers and sort codes that your accountant doesn't necessarily need — and may pass on to AI tools or other software. The anonymise guide covers how to do this in a few minutes.

items.title: How openstan helps
items.text:
If you have statements from more than one account, or you're doing this for the first time and want a safety net, openstan handles the mechanical parts of this workflow:

  • Gap detection — flags any missing months after you import, across all accounts simultaneously
  • Multi-account support — imports PDFs from HSBC, NatWest, TSB and others in one batch, keeping each account separate
  • Balance verification — checks that opening and closing balances match between consecutive statements, catching incomplete downloads before they cause problems later
  • Export to Excel or CSV — produces a clean flat file your accountant can filter and sort

See the Self Assessment use case for a full walkthrough, or the Export Bank Statements from Multiple Accounts guide for step-by-step instructions.

items.title: How long to keep your statements
items.text:
GOV.UK states that self-employed taxpayers must keep records for at least 5 years after the 31 January submission deadline for the relevant tax year.

In practice: if you filed your 2022–23 return by 31 January 2024, keep all supporting records until at least 31 January 2029.

If you sent your return more than 4 years after the deadline, you must keep records for 15 months after the date you filed.

If your records are lost, stolen, or destroyed, GOV.UK advises you to do your best to provide figures and tell HMRC if you're using estimated or provisional figures when you file.

Keep original PDFs. An openstan export is useful for working with the data, but it is not a substitute for the official bank statements if HMRC requests records.

items.title: FAQ
items.text:
Do I need to send bank statements with my tax return? No. GOV.UK states this directly: "You do not need to send your records in when you submit your tax return." You keep them and produce them if HMRC asks.

What if I changed banks mid-year? Include statements from both banks for the full tax year, covering the dates when each account was active. Make sure there's no gap between them.

What if a statement is missing? Contact your bank and request a reissue. Banks vary in how long they retain records and whether they charge for older statements — check with your bank directly. Allow several working days for the request to be processed.

Do I need to include personal transactions if I use a personal account for business? GOV.UK notes that you might use a personal or business bank account for your business. If business income or expenses pass through a personal account, you'll need records covering those transactions. The cleanest solution going forward is a dedicated business account.

Can HMRC check my bank records? Yes. GOV.UK's tax compliance checks page explains that HMRC may check your records to make sure you're paying the right amount of tax. This can include your Self Assessment return. If HMRC contacts you about a compliance check, GOV.UK advises you can have an accountant or legal adviser with you, and you can apply for alternative dispute resolution if you disagree with their findings.

items.title: Connecting HSBC Configs Together — The statement_types & standard_fields Layer
items.text: We've built companies.toml, accounts.toml, and statement_tables.toml. We know how to identify the bank, detect the account type, extract balances, and parse transactions. But how do they all work together? The final layer is statement_types.toml, which orchestrates the extraction pipeline. And then we map raw extracted fields to standard output columns using standard_fields.toml. This post brings everything together.
path: Connecting HSBC Configs Together — The statement_types & standard_fields Layer

items.title: Connecting HSBC Configs Together — The statement_types & standard_fields Layer

items.title: The Big Picture: Five Config Files, One Complete Parser
items.text:
Let's zoom out and see the entire architecture:

Input: Unknown PDF file
    ↓
companies.toml (Post #1)
  Identify bank: "HSBC_UK" ✓
    ↓
accounts.toml (Post #2)
  Identify account type: "HSBC_UK_CUR_STD" ✓
    ↓
statement_types.toml (Post #4 — this post)
  Choose extraction strategy: "HSBC_UK_CUR"
    ↓
statement_tables.toml (Posts #2–3)
  Extract data using 4 tables:
    - Company info (identification)
    - Account summary (balances)
    - Account details (account holder info)
    - Transactions (line items)
    ↓
standard_fields.toml (Post #4 — this post)
  Map raw fields to standardized output:
    - raw 'date' → STD_DATE (ISO 8601)
    - raw '£_paid_in' → STD_AMOUNT
    - raw 'details' → STD_DESCRIPTION
    ↓
Output: Standardized transaction records (CSV, JSON, Parquet)

Each layer depends on the previous one. If company detection fails, nothing else runs. If account detection fails, the parser can't load the right extraction rules. This modular architecture means:

  • Reusability: Multiple account types use the same statement_type and tables (e.g., both CUR_STD and CUR_ADV use HSBC_UK_CUR)
  • Maintainability: Each file has a clear responsibility
  • Extensibility: Adding a new bank or account type doesn't require touching old configs
path: Connecting HSBC Configs Together — The statement_types & standard_fields Layer

items.title: Introducing statement_types.toml
items.text:
After account detection succeeds, the parser needs to know how to extract data. This is the job of statement_types.toml.

Purpose: Group extraction rules into two sections — header and lines.

Here's HSBC's complete statement_types.toml (all 3 account types: current, savings, credit card):

[HSBC_UK_CUR]
statement_type = 'HSBC UK Current Account'
    [HSBC_UK_CUR.header]
        [[HSBC_UK_CUR.header.configs]]
            config = 'Company Info'
            locations = [
                {page_number = 1, top_left = [475,110], bottom_right = [575, 130]},
                {page_number = 1, top_left = [460,145], bottom_right = [575, 165]},
                {page_number = 1, top_left = [460,165], bottom_right = [575, 185]},
            ]
            field = {field = 'website', vital=true, type="string", string_pattern ='^www\.hsbc\.co\.uk$'}

        [[HSBC_UK_CUR.header.configs]]
            config = 'Statement Info'
            locations = [{page_number=1, top_left = [37, 325], bottom_right = [290, 385]}]
            field = {field = 'statement_date', vital=true, type = "string", string_pattern ='^[1-3]?[0-9]\s[A-Z][a-z]{2,8}\s(\d{4}\s)?to\s[1-3]?[0-9]\s[A-Z][a-z]{2,8}\s[0-9]{4}$'}

        [[HSBC_UK_CUR.header.configs]]
            config = 'Account Info'
            statement_table_key = 'HSBC_UK_CUR_ACCT_SUM'

        [[HSBC_UK_CUR.header.configs]]
            config = 'Account Details'
            statement_table_key = 'HSBC_UK_CUR_ACCT_DET'

    [HSBC_UK_CUR.lines]
        [[HSBC_UK_CUR.lines.configs]]
            config = 'Transaction Lines'
            statement_table_key = 'HSBC_UK_CUR_TRANSACTIONS'

[HSBC_UK_SAV]
statement_type = 'HSBC UK Saving Account'
    [HSBC_UK_SAV.header]
        [[HSBC_UK_SAV.header.configs]]
            config = 'Statement Balances'
            statement_table_key = 'HSBC_UK_CUR_ACCT_SUM'

        [[HSBC_UK_SAV.header.configs]]
            config = 'Statement Info'
            locations = [{page_number=1, top_left = [37, 325], bottom_right = [290, 385]}]
            field = {field = 'statement_date', vital=true, type = "string", string_pattern ='^[1-3]?[0-9]\s[A-Z][a-z]{2,8}\s(\d{4}\s)?to\s[1-3]?[0-9]\s[A-Z][a-z]{2,8}\s[0-9]{4}$'}

        [[HSBC_UK_SAV.header.configs]]
            config = 'Account Info'
            statement_table_key = 'HSBC_UK_SAV_ACCT_DET'

    [HSBC_UK_SAV.lines]
        [[HSBC_UK_SAV.lines.configs]]
            config = 'Transaction Lines'
            statement_table_key = 'HSBC_UK_CUR_TRANSACTIONS'

[HSBC_UK_CRD]
statement_type = 'HSBC UK Credit Card'
    [HSBC_UK_CRD.header]
        [[HSBC_UK_CRD.header.configs]]
            config = 'Statement Balances'
            statement_table_key = 'HSBC_UK_CRD_ACCT_SUM'

        [[HSBC_UK_CRD.header.configs]]
            config = 'Statement Info'
            locations = [{page_number=1, top_left = [120, 470], bottom_right = [250, 500]}]
            field = {field = 'statement_date', vital=true, type = "string", string_pattern ='^[0-3]?[0-9]\s[A-Z][a-z]{2,8}\s[0-9]{4}$'}

        [[HSBC_UK_CRD.header.configs]]
            config = 'Account Info'
            locations = [{page_number=2, top_left = [44, 174], bottom_right = [215, 200]}]
            field = {field = 'account_name', vital=true, type = "string", string_pattern ='^[A-Z]+[a-z]*\s[A-Z]+[a-z]*.*$'}

        [[HSBC_UK_CRD.header.configs]]
            config = 'Card Number'
            locations = [{page_number=2, top_left = [220, 175], bottom_right = [340, 197]}]
            field = {field = 'card_number', vital=true, type = "string", string_pattern ='^[0-9]{4}\s[0-9]{4}\s[0-9]{4}\s[0-9]{4}\s?$'}

    [HSBC_UK_CRD.lines]
        [[HSBC_UK_CRD.lines.configs]]
            config = 'Transaction Lines'
            statement_table_key = 'HSBC_UK_CRD_TRANSACTIONS'

Let's break down what's happening:

[HSBC_UK_CUR] — Identifier (must match statement_type_key in accounts.toml). When the parser identifies account HSBC_UK_CUR_STD, it looks up its statement_type_key = 'HSBC_UK_CUR' and loads this section.

statement_type = 'HSBC UK Current Account' — Human-readable label (used in logs and output).

.header section — Extraction steps that run once per statement (usually from page 1): - Company info (bank identification) - Statement info (statement date range) - Account summary (opening/closing balances) - Account details (account holder name, sort code, account number)

.lines section — Extraction steps that run on every page: - Transaction lines (individual transactions)

items.title: Separating Header & Lines
items.text:
Why have two sections?

Header — Runs once - Extracts statement-level metadata (opening balance, statement period, account info) - Usually on page 1 (sometimes page 2 for multi-page statements) - Example: "This is HSBC, it's John Smith's account, 01 Jan to 31 Jan, opening balance 5000"

Lines — Runs on every page - Extracts data that repeats (transactions) - Applied to pages 1, 2, 3, etc. - Example: "50 transactions across 3 pages"

Benefit: Efficiency. You don't re-extract the opening balance from every page.

Diagram:

Statement with 3 pages:

Page 1: [Header extraction + Lines extraction]
        Extract: balance, account info, 15 transactions

Page 2: [Lines extraction only]
        Extract: 20 transactions

Page 3: [Lines extraction only]
        Extract: 15 transactions

Result: 1 set of metadata + 50 total transactions
path: Connecting HSBC Configs Together — The statement_types & standard_fields Layer

items.title: What About Different Account Types?
items.text:
Notice that HSBC_UK_CUR and HSBC_UK_SAV are mostly the same, but HSBC_UK_CRD (credit card) is different:

HSBC_UK_CUR (current account): - Header: Company info, statement date, account summary (HSBC_UK_CUR_ACCT_SUM), account details - Lines: Transactions (HSBC_UK_CUR_TRANSACTIONS)

HSBC_UK_CRD (credit card): - Header: Company info, statement date, account summary (HSBC_UK_CRD_ACCT_SUM), account name, card number - Lines: Transactions (HSBC_UK_CRD_TRANSACTIONS)

Differences: - Credit cards use different balance tables (credit limit, APR, minimum payment instead of opening balance) - Account info is on page 2, not page 1 (note page_number=2) - Card number extraction is specific to credit cards

Key insight: Same bank, different statement_types for different products. Each gets its own extraction strategy tailored to that product's PDF layout.
path: Connecting HSBC Configs Together — The statement_types & standard_fields Layer

items.title: Mapping Raw Fields to Standard Output: standard_fields.toml
items.text:
After extraction, we have raw fields with bank-specific names and formats: - Raw field: date = "03 Jan" - Raw field: payment_type = "CHQ" - Raw field: £_paid_in = "2500.00"

But downstream systems (openstan, accounting software, Excel) need standardized fields: - Standard field: STD_DATE = "2026-01-03" (ISO 8601) - Standard field: STD_AMOUNT = "2500.00" - Standard field: STD_DESCRIPTION = "TESCO CARDIFF"

The standard_fields.toml file maps raw → standard. Here's an example:

[[std_refs]]
statement_type = "HSBC UK Current Account"
config = "Transaction Lines"

[std_refs.standard_fields]
STD_DATE = {from = "date", format = "DD MMM YY"}
STD_AMOUNT = {from = "£_paid_in", default = 0}
STD_AMOUNT_OUT = {from = "£_paid_out", default = 0}
STD_BALANCE = {from = "£_balance"}
STD_DESCRIPTION = {from = "details"}
STD_COMPANY = "HSBC Bank UK"
STD_ACCOUNT_NAME = {from = "account_name"}
STD_SORTCODE = {from = "sortcode"}
STD_ACCOUNT_NUMBER = {from = "account_number"}

Each mapping has a type:

STD_DATE = {from = "date", format = "DD MMM YY"} — Extract from raw field "date", parse using format "DD MMM YY", output as ISO 8601

STD_AMOUNT = {from = "£_paid_in", default = 0} — Extract from raw field "£_paid_in"; if empty, use default 0

STD_COMPANY = "HSBC Bank UK" — Hardcoded value (not extracted from PDF)

STD_ACCOUNT_NAME = {from = "account_name"} — Extract from raw field "account_name", pass through as-is

Why this layer matters:

Your parser is bank-specific. HSBC uses different field names and formats than NatWest. But your users want consistent output regardless of bank. Standard fields provide that consistency.
path: Connecting HSBC Configs Together — The statement_types & standard_fields Layer

items.title: Date Format Transformations
items.text:
HSBC transactions have dates like "03 Jan". Your output needs ISO 8601 format: "2026-01-03".

The format parameter tells the parser how to interpret HSBC's format: - DD = 2-digit day (01–31) - MMM = 3-letter month (Jan, Feb, Mar, etc.) - YY = 2-digit year (00–99, interpreted as 2000–2099)

Parser extracts "03 Jan", interprets as day=3, month=1, year=26, outputs "2026-01-03".

Why different banks need different formats:

Different banks use different date notation: - HSBC: "03 Jan" (day space month) - NatWest: "03/01/26" (day/month/year) - Barclays: "03-JAN-26" (day-month-year)

Standard_fields.toml handles these differences with appropriate format strings. The final output is always ISO 8601.
path: Connecting HSBC Configs Together — The statement_types & standard_fields Layer

items.title: Handling Bank-Specific Quirks
items.text:
Some fields are bank-specific:

STD_CREDIT_LIMIT = {from = "credit_limit"}  # Only for credit cards
STD_INTEREST_RATE = {from = "apr"}  # Only for savings/credit cards

For each statement_type, you define which fields are relevant. The parser only extracts fields that exist in that statement_type's config.

Static fields:

STD_COMPANY = "HSBC Bank UK"  # Same for all HSBC transactions
STD_ACCOUNT_TYPE = "Current Account"  # Varies by account type

Fields with defaults:

STD_AMOUNT = {from = "£_paid_in", default = 0}

If a transaction has no paid_in value (empty field), use 0. This handles cases where only paid_out has a value.

items.title: End-to-End Validation: From PDF to Standardized Output
items.text:
Here's the complete flow for a single transaction:

Step 1: Extract raw fields (statement_tables.toml) 

Raw: date="03 Jan", type="CHQ", details="TESCO CARDIFF", 
     out=50.00, in=empty, balance=7450.00 D

Step 2: Parse and validate (field-level rules) 

date matches pattern? ✓
type matches pattern? ✓
details not empty? ✓
amount is numeric? ✓
balance is numeric? ✓

Step 3: Map to standard fields (standard_fields.toml) 

STD_DATE = parse "03 Jan" with "DD MMM YY" → "2026-01-03"
STD_AMOUNT = £_paid_in = empty, default to 0 → 0.00
STD_AMOUNT_OUT = £_paid_out = 50.00 → 50.00
STD_BALANCE = £_balance = 7450.00 (with D suffix, multiply by -1) → -7450.00
STD_DESCRIPTION = details = "TESCO CARDIFF" → "TESCO CARDIFF"
STD_COMPANY = hardcoded → "HSBC Bank UK"
STD_ACCOUNT_NAME = from account_name → "John Smith"

Step 4: Output (CSV, JSON, Parquet) 

STD_DATE,STD_COMPANY,STD_ACCOUNT_NAME,STD_AMOUNT,STD_AMOUNT_OUT,STD_BALANCE,STD_DESCRIPTION
2026-01-03,HSBC Bank UK,John Smith,0.00,50.00,-7450.00,TESCO CARDIFF

Every transaction goes through this pipeline. The result: consistent, standardized output regardless of the input bank.

items.title: Extending to Multiple Account Types: The Complete Picture
items.text:
HSBC_UK has 5 account types. Each has:

Component HSBC_UK_CUR_STD HSBC_UK_CUR_ADV HSBC_UK_SAV_FLX HSBC_UK_CRD_RCC accounts.toml ✓ Account config ✓ Account config ✓ Account config ✓ Account config statement_types.toml HSBC_UK_CUR HSBC_UK_CUR HSBC_UK_SAV HSBC_UK_CRD statement_tables.toml CUR_ACCT_SUM, CUR_ACCT_DET, CUR_TRANSACTIONS (same as CUR_STD) SAV_ACCT_DET, CUR_TRANSACTIONS CRD_ACCT_SUM, CRD_TRANSACTIONS standard_fields.toml Mapping for HSBC_UK_CUR (same as CUR_STD) Mapping for HSBC_UK_SAV Mapping for HSBC_UK_CRD

Notice reuse: Both CUR_STD and CUR_ADV use the same statement_type, tables, and standard fields (they have the same PDF layout).

The parser handles this automatically: 1. Identify company: HSBC_UK 2. Identify account: HSBC_UK_CUR_STD or HSBC_UK_CUR_ADV? 3. Load statement_type: HSBC_UK_CUR (same for both) 4. Extract using that strategy 5. Map to standard fields using HSBC_UK_CUR mapping

items.title: Common Integration Issues & Troubleshooting
items.text:
Q: Statements extract but dates are wrong in CSV

A: Check standard_fields.toml date format. If you said format = "DD MMM YY" but your PDF actually has "MM/DD/YYYY", dates will be misinterpreted. Test with a known transaction and verify the output.

Q: Some accounts extract but others don't

A: Likely different account types with different statement_types. Verify that the account's statement_type_key in accounts.toml points to a valid section in statement_types.toml. Missing or misspelled references will fail silently.

Q: Balance reconciliation fails (opening + movements ≠ closing)

A: Check numeric_modifiers on balance fields. HSBC uses "D" suffix to indicate inverted balances. If your numeric_modifier isn't applied correctly, reconciliation will fail. Enable debug logging to see calculated vs extracted balances.

Q: Transactions missing from output

A: Check the delete_* flags in statement_tables.toml. If strict validation is enabled, some transactions might be filtered out. Enable debug logging to see which rows were deleted and why.

items.title: Now It's Your Turn: Putting It All Together
items.text:
You've learned the full stack. Here's the checklist to build a complete parser for your bank:

✓ Post #1: Create companies.toml (bank identification) ✓ Post #2: Create accounts.toml + statement_tables.toml for summary (account identification + balance extraction) ✓ Post #3: Extend statement_tables.toml with transaction table config ✓ Post #4: Create statement_types.toml (orchestration) and standard_fields.toml (output mapping)

Validation workflow:

  1. Test company detection: 

    python -m bank_statement_parser identify path/to/pdf.pdf
    Expected: "HSBC_UK" (or your bank)

  2. Test account detection: 

    python -m bank_statement_parser import path/to/pdf.pdf --dry-run
    Expected: Account type identified, extraction strategy loaded

  3. Test full extraction: 

    python -m bank_statement_parser import path/to/pdf.pdf --output=csv
    Expected: CSV with all standard fields populated

  4. Verify output:

  5. Check dates are ISO 8601
  6. Check amounts are numeric and correct sign
  7. Check balances reconcile

  8. Check descriptions are readable

  9. Iterate:

  10. Adjust regex patterns if validation fails
  11. Adjust coordinates if tables aren't found
  12. Adjust field mappings if output is wrong

  13. Re-test after each change

  14. Submit PR:

  15. Test thoroughly with 5–10 different statements
  16. Anonymize test PDFs (remove account numbers, names)
  17. Create PR to bank_statement_parser repository
  18. Include test PDFs and brief description of changes

Q: Why do I need both statement_types.toml AND accounts.toml?

A: accounts.toml identifies which specific account this is (CUR_STD vs CRD_RCC). statement_types.toml defines the extraction strategy. The separation allows multiple accounts to use the same extraction strategy (e.g., both CUR_STD and CUR_ADV use HSBC_UK_CUR).

Q: How do I test my standard_fields mapping?

A: Run extraction with --output=csv and inspect the results. Check that: - Dates are properly formatted (ISO 8601) - Amounts match the PDF - Descriptions are readable - No data is truncated or missing

Q: What if my bank has variable PDF layouts (different designs for different statement dates)?

A: Add multiple statement_type entries or use pdfplumber's allow_text_failover to handle variations. Document known variations in your contribution PR.

items.title: Extracting HSBC Account Details — From Current to Savings to Credit Cards
items.text: Now that we can identify an HSBC PDF, the next challenge is figuring out what kind of account it is. HSBC offers current accounts, savings accounts, credit cards, and ISAs—all with different PDF layouts. We built account-type detection and balance extraction using two more TOML files. Here's how.

items.title: The Problem: One Bank, Multiple Account Types
items.text:
Imagine you've successfully identified a PDF as HSBC_UK (from Post #1). But now what? HSBC's current account statements look completely different from their savings account statements, which look different again from their credit card statements. Same bank, three different layouts.

Your parser needs to know: - Which account type is this? (Current, Savings, Credit Card, etc.) - Where are the balances? (Different tables for different products) - What fields are available? (Credit cards have "Credit Limit" and "APR"; current accounts have "Opening Balance")

If you use current-account extraction rules on a credit card statement, the parser will fail—it's looking for fields that don't exist in that layout.

This is where accounts.toml and account-specific tables come in. After company detection (Post #1), your parser runs account detection. It tries each account type until one matches.

items.title: Identifying Account Type with accounts.toml
items.text:
Here's HSBC's complete accounts.toml file. It has 5 different account types, each with its own config:

[HSBC_UK_CUR_STD]
account = "Bank Account"
company_key = 'HSBC_UK'
account_type_key = 'CUR'
statement_type_key = 'HSBC_UK_CUR'
exclude_last_n_pages = 1
currency = "GBP"
    [HSBC_UK_CUR_STD.config]
    config = 'Account Info'
    locations = [{page_number = 1, top_left = [37, 400], bottom_right = [255, 465]}]
    field = {field = 'account', vital=true, type = "string", string_pattern = '^(Your[\s])?Bank[\s]*Account'}

[HSBC_UK_CUR_ADV]
account = "HSBC Advance"
company_key = 'HSBC_UK'
account_type_key = 'CUR'
statement_type_key = 'HSBC_UK_CUR'
exclude_last_n_pages = 1
currency = "GBP"
    [HSBC_UK_CUR_ADV.config]
    config = 'Account Info'
    locations = [{page_number = 1, top_left = [25, 400], bottom_right = [270, 445]}]
    field = {field = 'account', vital=true, type = "string", string_pattern = '^Your[\s]*HSBC[\s]*Advance'}

[HSBC_UK_SAV_FLX]
account = "Flexible Saver"
company_key = 'HSBC_UK'
account_type_key = 'SAV'
statement_type_key = 'HSBC_UK_SAV'
exclude_last_n_pages = 1
currency = "GBP"
    [HSBC_UK_SAV_FLX.config]
    config = 'Account Info'
    locations = [{page_number = 1, top_left = [37, 425], bottom_right = [255, 480]}]
    field = {field = 'account', vital=true, type = "string", string_pattern = '^Your[\s]*Flexible[\s]*Saver'}

[HSBC_UK_SAV_OBS]
account = "Online Bonus Saver"
company_key = 'HSBC_UK'
account_type_key = 'SAV'
statement_type_key = 'HSBC_UK_SAV'
exclude_last_n_pages = 1
currency = "GBP"
    [HSBC_UK_SAV_OBS.config]
    config = 'Account Info'
    locations = [{page_number = 1, top_left = [37, 425], bottom_right = [255, 490]}]
    field = {field = 'account', vital=true, type = "string", string_pattern = '^(Your[\s])?Online[\s]*Bonus[\s]*Saver'}

[HSBC_UK_CRD_RCC]
account = "Rewards Credit Card"
company_key = 'HSBC_UK'
account_type_key = 'CRD'
statement_type_key = 'HSBC_UK_CRD'
exclude_last_n_pages = 1
currency = "GBP"
    [HSBC_UK_CRD_RCC.config]
    config = 'Account Info'
    locations = [{page_number = 1, top_left = [275, 20], bottom_right = [575, 70]}]
    field = {field = 'account', vital=true, type="string", string_pattern ='^Your[\s]*Rewards[\s]*Credit[\s]*Card[\s]*statement[\s]*'}

That's 5 account types, all from the same bank (HSBC_UK). Let's break down what each field means:

[HSBC_UK_CUR_STD] — Unique account ID (must be unique across all banks and accounts in your project). Think of it as the account's fingerprint. This ID is used throughout the config system to link to extraction rules.

account = "Bank Account" — Human-readable name (the actual product name from HSBC's marketing). Used in logs and output.

company_key = 'HSBC_UK' — Links this account to the company from Post #1. Must match the [HSBC_UK] section in companies.toml.

account_type_key = 'CUR' — Account type code. Standard codes are: - CUR = Current Account - SAV = Savings Account - CRD = Credit Card - ISA = ISA (tax-advantaged savings)

This is registered in account_types.toml (which we won't detail here, but it's just a lookup table of codes to names).

statement_type_key = 'HSBC_UK_CUR' — Links to extraction strategy (covered in Post #4). Different account types use different statement types. Notice that both CUR_STD and CUR_ADV use the same statement_type (HSBC_UK_CUR) because they have the same PDF layout. But credit cards (CRD_RCC) use HSBC_UK_CRD because their layout is different.

exclude_last_n_pages = 1 — Ignore the last page when extracting. HSBC typically puts T&Cs and marketing on the final page, which we don't want to parse.

currency = "GBP" — Account currency (used for numeric parsing). All HSBC_UK accounts are GBP, but if your bank offers multi-currency, this varies per account.

.config section — Account-type detection logic (similar to company detection from Post #1): - locations — where on the page to look (page 1, specific bounding box) - field — what to extract and validate

The regex pattern for HSBC_UK_CUR_STD is: ^(Your[\s])?Bank[\s]*Account

This matches: - ✓ "Bank Account" (no "Your") - ✓ "Your Bank Account" (with "Your") - ✓ "Your Bank Account" (flexible whitespace) - ✗ "Your Savings Account" (doesn't match, so this account type isn't selected)

items.title: Why Multiple Account Types in One Config File?
items.text:
HSBC has 5 account types in a single accounts.toml. The parser tries each one in order until one matches:

  1. Try HSBC_UK_CUR_STD: Search for "Bank Account" pattern
  2. If found → This is a current account, use HSBC_UK_CUR extraction strategy
  3. Try HSBC_UK_CUR_ADV: Search for "HSBC Advance" pattern
  4. If found → This is an advance account, use HSBC_UK_CUR extraction strategy
  5. Try HSBC_UK_SAV_FLX: Search for "Flexible Saver" pattern
  6. If found → This is a savings account, use HSBC_UK_SAV extraction strategy
  7. Try HSBC_UK_SAV_OBS: Search for "Online Bonus Saver" pattern
  8. If found → This is a savings account, use HSBC_UK_SAV extraction strategy
  9. Try HSBC_UK_CRD_RCC: Search for "Credit Card" pattern
  10. If found → This is a credit card, use HSBC_UK_CRD extraction strategy

Same bank (HSBC_UK), different account types, different extraction strategies. It's like a decision tree: "I found an HSBC PDF. Now, is it this product, or this product, or this one?"
