items.title: Extracting Account Balances with statement_tables.toml
items.text:
We've identified the account type. Now we need to extract data. This is where statement_tables.toml comes in.

There are three types of tables in a bank statement: - Summary tables — Fixed-structure tables with known row/column positions (opening balance, payments in/out, closing balance) - Detail tables — Account-holder info (name, sort code, account number) - Transaction tables — Variable-length transaction rows (covered in detail in Post #3)

For now, we're focused on summary and detail tables. Here's the HSBC current account summary table config:

[HSBC_UK_CUR_ACCT_SUM]
type = "summary"
statement_table = 'Account Summary'
table_columns = 2
table_rows = 4
row_spacing = 7
locations = [
    {page_number=1, top_left = [345, 180], bottom_right = [575, 300], 
     vertical_lines = [360, 475, 475, 550], 
     dynamic_last_vertical_line = {image_id = 0, image_location_tag = "x1"}, 
     allow_text_failover = true},
]
fields = [
    {field = 'opening_balance', cell = {row = 1, col = 1}, vital=true, type = 'currency', numeric_modifier = {suffix = "D", multiplier = -1}},
    {field = 'payments_in', cell = {row = 2, col = 1}, vital=true, type = 'currency'},
    {field = 'payments_out', cell = {row = 3, col = 1}, vital=true, type = 'currency'},
    {field = 'closing_balance', cell = {row = 4, col = 1}, vital=true, type = 'currency', numeric_modifier = {suffix = "D", multiplier = -1}},
]

type = "summary" — This is a fixed-structure table (not variable-length transactions).

statement_table = 'Account Summary' — Label for this table (for logs).

table_columns = 2 — Expected number of columns (Account Summary typically has 2: a label column and a value column).

table_rows = 4 — Expected number of rows (opening balance, payments in, payments out, closing balance = 4 rows).

row_spacing = 7 — PDF row spacing tolerance. If two rows are within 7 PDF points of each other vertically, they're considered part of the same visual row. This handles slight PDF formatting variations.

locations — Where to find the table: - page_number=1 — On page 1 - top_left = [345, 180] — Top-left corner at x=345, y=180 - bottom_right = [575, 300] — Bottom-right corner at x=575, y=300 - vertical_lines = [360, 475, 475, 550] — Column boundaries at x=360, x=475, and x=550 - Column 0: x=360 to x=475 (labels like "Opening Balance") - Column 1: x=475 to x=550 (values like "5,000.00") - The pair [475, 475] creates a hard column boundary - dynamic_last_vertical_line = {image_id = 0, image_location_tag = "x1"} — The right edge (x1) of image 0 is used as the rightmost column boundary. Why? HSBC has a logo on the right side of the table, and its position varies slightly. Instead of hardcoding x=550, we let the logo's right edge define the boundary. Smart! - allow_text_failover = true — If column detection fails, try again without explicit vertical_lines. Fall back to pdfplumber's automatic column detection as a safety net.

fields — What to extract from each cell: - field = 'opening_balance' — Field name - cell = {row = 1, col = 1} — Zero-indexed: row 1 = 2nd row, col 1 = 2nd column - vital=true — Extraction failure means the whole statement fails - type = 'currency' — Parse as a currency value - numeric_modifier = {suffix = "D", multiplier = -1} — If value ends with "D" (debit), multiply by -1 (explained below)

items.title: Cell Addressing & Coordinates Explained
items.text:
Cell addressing uses 1-based row indexing in this config, so row 1 is the first row of the table:

Row Col 0 Col 1 1 "Opening Balance" 5,000.00 CR 2 "Payments In" 2,500.00 3 "Payments Out" 1,200.50 4 "Closing Balance" 6,300.00 D So cell = {row = 1, col = 1} points to "2,500.00" (the second row, second column).

The vertical_lines define column boundaries. In HSBC's config: [360, 475, 475, 550]

This creates: - Column 0: x=360 to x=475 (labels) - Column 1: x=475 to x=550 (values)

The pair [475, 475] is special—it's a zero-width boundary that forces a hard column split. Without it, pdfplumber might merge columns if they're close together. With it, we're saying: "Even if there's no visual gap, treat x=475 as a hard boundary."
path: Extracting HSBC Account Details — From Current to Savings to Credit Cards

items.title: The Mysterious "D" Modifier: Debit vs Credit
items.text:
Here's something you'll encounter with HSBC: balance fields are marked with a suffix—either "CR" (credit) or "D" (debit).

  • "CR" or "D" = Negative balance (you owe money, or the balance is inverted in accounting terms)
  • Regular number = Positive balance (you have money)

This is HSBC's notation, but it's unusual. Most systems expect: - Positive number = you have money - Negative number = you owe money

The numeric_modifier solves this:

numeric_modifier = {suffix = "D", multiplier = -1}

This says: "If the extracted value ends with 'D', strip the 'D' and multiply by -1."

Example: - Raw from PDF: "5,000.00 D" - After extraction: 5,000.00 (numeric) - Check suffix: ends with "D"? Yes - Apply multiplier: 5,000.00 × -1 = -5,000.00 - Final value: -5,000.00

Downstream systems expect this sign convention, so this transformation is crucial. Without it, you'd have inverted balances (positive when they should be negative, and vice versa).
path: Extracting HSBC Account Details — From Current to Savings to Credit Cards

items.title: Account Detail Tables: Sort Code, Account Number, Name
items.text:
Beyond balances, we also need to extract account holder info. Here's the account detail table config:

[HSBC_UK_CUR_ACCT_DET]
type = "detail"
statement_table = 'Account Details'
table_columns = 4
table_rows = 2
locations = [
    {page_number = 1, top_left = [37, 365], bottom_right = [575, 410], vertical_lines = [52, 355, 414, 493, 557]},
]
fields = [
    {field = 'account_name', cell = {row = 1, col = 0}, vital = true, type = "string", string_pattern ='^[A-Z]+[a-z]*\s[A-Z]+[a-z]*.*$'},
    {field = 'sortcode', cell = {row = 1, col = 1}, vital=true, type = "string", string_pattern ='^[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$'},
    {field = 'account_number', cell = {row = 1, col = 2}, vital=true, type = "string", string_pattern ='^[0-9]{8}$'},
]

Same structure as the summary table, but we're extracting account holder details. Each field has a regex pattern to validate:

  • account_name: ^[A-Z]+[a-z]*\s[A-Z]+[a-z]*.*$
  • Matches: "John Smith", "Jane Doe", "A B"
  • Requires at least 2 capital-letter words

  • Accounts for names like "McDonald Smith" (mixed case)

  • sortcode: ^[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}$

  • Matches: "12-34-56" (UK sort code format: 2-2-2 digits)

  • Exactly 6 digits with hyphens in the right places

  • account_number: ^[0-9]{8}$

  • Matches: "12345678" (UK account numbers are always 8 digits)
  • Exactly 8 digits, no more, no less

If a field doesn't match its pattern, extraction is marked as failed. With vital=true, the entire statement fails. This catches parsing errors early and prevents garbage data from reaching your output.

items.title: Putting It Together: The Flow
items.text:
Here's the complete account detection + extraction flow:

  1. Company detection succeeds (Post #1) → Identified as HSBC_UK
  2. Account detection starts:
  3. Try HSBC_UK_CUR_STD: Search for "Bank Account" pattern on page 1
  4. Pattern matches! Account type identified as HSBC_UK_CUR_STD
  5. Load account configuration:
  6. account_type_key = 'CUR' (current account)
  7. statement_type_key = 'HSBC_UK_CUR' (use this extraction strategy)
  8. Extract balances using HSBC_UK_CUR_ACCT_SUM table
  9. Crop to [345,180] → [575,300]
  10. Extract opening_balance from cell [1,1]: "5,000.00 D"
  11. Apply numeric_modifier: convert to -5,000.00
  12. Extract payments_in, payments_out, closing_balance similarly
  13. Extract account details using HSBC_UK_CUR_ACCT_DET table
  14. Extract account_name, sortcode, account_number
  15. Validate against regex patterns
  16. If all vital fields pass validation: success
  17. Continue to transaction extraction (Post #3)

items.title: Common Issues & Solutions
items.text:
Q: Why do some HSBC accounts have different balance table positions?

A: Different account types (current vs savings vs credit card) have different PDF layouts. The balance table might be at different y-coordinates. Solution: use try_shift_down parameter to auto-adjust by a small amount if the first location fails.

Q: What if the account name pattern doesn't match my account?

A: Your account might have a different name format (titles, hyphens, etc.). Test the regex pattern against your actual PDF text, then adjust. The pattern ^[A-Z]+[a-z]*\s[A-Z]+[a-z]*.*$ is flexible, but modify it if needed.

Q: How do I find the correct pixel coordinates?

A: Use a PDF viewer with coordinate display, or use pdfplumber's Python API to programmatically find table positions. Trial and error is fine—test, check the output, adjust by 50 pixels, re-test. You'll converge quickly.

items.title: Parsing HSBC Transactions — Handling Multi-Row Transactions & Bookends
items.text: We've identified the bank and extracted account balances. Now comes the hardest part: transactions. HSBC packs each transaction into a table, but here's the problem: not every transaction is one row. Some transactions span 2–3 rows because the description wraps. Figuring out where one transaction ends and the next begins requires a clever technique called "bookend detection." Here's how we solved it.
path: Parsing HSBC Transactions — Handling Multi-Row Transactions & Bookends

items.title: Parsing HSBC Transactions — Handling Multi-Row Transactions & Bookends
path: Parsing HSBC Transactions — Handling Multi-Row Transactions & Bookends

items.title: The Multi-Row Transaction Problem
items.text:
Let's look at what a real HSBC transaction table looks like (simplified):

Row 1:  01 Jan | FPI      | SALARY EMPLOYER      | —    | 2500.00 | 7500.00
Row 2:  03 Jan | CHQ      | TESCO CARDIFF        | 50.00| —       | 7450.00
Row 3:  —     | —        | Reference continues  | —    | —       | —
Row 4:  05 Jan | TRF      | WATER BILL PAYMENT   | 150.00| —      | 7300.00
Row 5:  08 Jan | DD       | ELECTRICITY CO       | 85.00| —       | 7215.00
Row 6:  —     | —        | Account number 999   | —    | —       | —

Here's the challenge: - Row 1: One complete transaction (salary payment) - Rows 2–3: One transaction that spans two rows (payment + continuation) - Row 4: One complete transaction - Rows 5–6: One transaction that spans two rows

Your parser needs to group these correctly: - Transaction 1: Row 1 only - Transaction 2: Rows 2 + 3 combined - Transaction 3: Row 4 only - Transaction 4: Rows 5 + 6 combined

How do you know when to merge rows and when to split? This is where bookend detection comes in.
path: Parsing HSBC Transactions — Handling Multi-Row Transactions & Bookends

items.title: Understanding Transaction Table Concepts
items.text:
Before we dive into the config, let's define some terminology:

Transaction row — A single complete transaction (might span 1 or more PDF rows)

PDF row — A single line in the pdfplumber-extracted table. For multi-row transactions, multiple PDF rows belong to one transaction row.

Bookend — A marker that identifies where a transaction starts or ends. For HSBC: - Start bookend: A row where BOTH payment_type AND details have values (e.g., "CHQ" and "TESCO CARDIFF") - End bookend: A row where EITHER paid_out OR paid_in has a value (the actual amount)

Fill-forward fields — Fields that repeat across multi-row transactions. The date and payment type usually only appear on the first row of a multi-row transaction; we propagate them to subsequent rows.

Merge fields — Fields that need to be combined across rows. If a description spans two rows ("TESCO CARDIFF" on row 1 and "Reference continues" on row 2), we merge them into one field.

items.title: Introducing the Transaction Table Config
items.text:
Here's HSBC's complete transaction table config. It's large, so we'll break it down piece by piece:

[HSBC_UK_CUR_TRANSACTIONS]
type = "transaction"
statement_table = 'Transactions'
table_columns = 6
locations = [
    {vertical_lines = [50, 100, 100, 130, 130, 320, 320, 400, 400, 480, 480, 555]},
]
fields = [
    {field = 'date', column = 0, vital=false, type = "string", string_pattern ='^[0-3][0-9]\s?[A-Z][a-z]{2}\s?[0-3][0-9]$'},
    {field = 'payment_type', column = 1, vital=false, type = "string", string_pattern ='(^[A-Z0-9]{1,3}$)|(^[)]{3}$)'},
    {field = 'details', column = 2, vital=true, type = "string", string_pattern ='.+', string_max_length = 100},
    {field = '£_paid_out', column = 3, vital=false, type = "currency"},
    {field = '£_paid_in', column = 4, vital=false, type = "currency"},
    {field = '£_balance', column = 5, vital=false, type = "currency", numeric_modifier = {suffix = "D", multiplier = -1.0000}},
]
delete_success_false = true
delete_cast_success_false = true
delete_rows_with_missing_vital_fields = true

[HSBC_UK_CUR_TRANSACTIONS.transaction_spec]
transaction_bookends = [
    {start_fields = ['payment_type','details'], min_non_empty_start = 2, end_fields = ['£_paid_out','£_paid_in'], min_non_empty_end = 1}
]
fill_forward_fields = ['date','payment_type']
merge_fields = {fields=['details'], separator=' | '}

That's a lot! Let's start with the basics.

items.title: Finding Columns Using pdfplumber Coordinates
items.text:
The vertical_lines parameter defines column boundaries:

vertical_lines = [50, 100, 100, 130, 130, 320, 320, 400, 400, 480, 480, 555]

These x-coordinates come in pairs:

Column Range Meaning 0 50 → 100 Date column (50 PDF points wide) 1 100 → 130 Payment type column (30 points wide) 2 130 → 320 Details column (190 points wide) 3 320 → 400 Paid out column (80 points wide) 4 400 → 480 Paid in column (80 points wide) 5 480 → 555 Balance column (75 points wide)

The pair [320, 320] (identical x-coordinates) creates a zero-width boundary. This forces a hard column split, ensuring the Details column ends and the Paid Out column begins at exactly x=320, even if there's no visual gap.

Why not let pdfplumber auto-detect columns?

pdfplumber can automatically detect columns by looking for gaps in text, but PDF layouts are often imprecise. Explicit boundaries give you full control. If your bank's transaction table has inconsistent spacing, explicit lines ensure consistent extraction.

How do you find these coordinates?

Option 1: Use pdfplumber's visual debugging 

import pdfplumber

with pdfplumber.open("statement.pdf") as pdf:
    page = pdf.pages[0]
    table = page.extract_table()
    # Inspect page.width, table structure, etc.

Option 2: Manual measurement - Open your PDF in a viewer - Measure where each column starts/ends - Trial and error: test, adjust, re-test
path: Parsing HSBC Transactions — Handling Multi-Row Transactions & Bookends

items.title: Bookend Detection: Knowing Where Transactions Start & End
items.text:
This is the core logic that handles multi-row transactions. Here's how it works:

transaction_bookends = [
    {start_fields = ['payment_type','details'], min_non_empty_start = 2, end_fields = ['£_paid_out','£_paid_in'], min_non_empty_end = 1}
]

A bookend definition has four parts:

start_fields — Fields that mark a transaction start. For HSBC: ['payment_type','details']

min_non_empty_start — Minimum number of start_fields that must have values. For HSBC: 2

This means: A transaction starts when BOTH payment_type AND details have values.

end_fields — Fields that mark a transaction end. For HSBC: ['£_paid_out','£_paid_in']

min_non_empty_end — Minimum number of end_fields that must have values. For HSBC: 1

This means: A transaction ends when EITHER paid_out OR paid_in has a value.

Let's trace through our example:

Row 1: date=01 Jan | type=FPI | details=SALARY  | out=—   | in=2500 | bal=7500
  → Starts? type≠empty, details≠empty → YES (2 of 2 start fields)
  → Ends? out=empty, in≠empty → YES (1 of 2 end fields)
  → Result: This is a 1-row transaction ✓
  → Extract: Transaction { date: 01 Jan, type: FPI, details: SALARY, in: 2500, bal: 7500 }

Row 2: date=03 Jan | type=CHQ | details=TESCO   | out=50  | in=—    | bal=7450
  → Starts? type≠empty, details≠empty → YES
  → Ends? out≠empty, in=empty → YES (1 of 2 end fields)
  → Result: This row starts a new transaction ✓

Row 3: date=—     | type=—   | details=contd... | out=—   | in=—    | bal=—
  → Starts? type=empty, details≠empty → NO (need BOTH; only have 1 of 2)
  → Ends? out=empty, in=empty → NO
  → Result: This row doesn't start or end a transaction
  → Conclusion: Row 3 continues the previous transaction (Row 2)
  → Merge with Row 2 ✓
  → Extract: Transaction { date: 03 Jan, type: CHQ, details: TESCO | contd..., out: 50, bal: 7450 }

Row 4: date=05 Jan | type=TRF | details=WATER   | out=150 | in=—    | bal=7300
  → Starts? type≠empty, details≠empty → YES
  → Ends? out≠empty → YES
  → Result: This is a 1-row transaction ✓
  → Extract: Transaction { date: 05 Jan, type: TRF, details: WATER, out: 150, bal: 7300 }

Row 5: date=08 Jan | type=DD  | details=ELEC    | out=85  | in=—    | bal=7215
  → Starts? type≠empty, details≠empty → YES

Row 6: date=—     | type=—   | details=Account | out=—   | in=—    | bal=—
  → Starts? type=empty → NO
  → Merge with Row 5 ✓
  → Extract: Transaction { date: 08 Jan, type: DD, details: ELEC | Account, out: 85, bal: 7215 }

Result: 4 transactions extracted correctly, with multi-row transactions merged.

Why this strategy works:

  • Start fields (payment_type, details) only appear on the first line of a transaction
  • Amount fields (paid_out, paid_in) only appear on the last line
  • Continuation rows have empty values for these fields
  • By checking these markers, we can identify transaction boundaries without hardcoding line counts
path: Parsing HSBC Transactions — Handling Multi-Row Transactions & Bookends

items.title: Fill-Forward Fields: Repeating Values Across Rows
items.text:
In multi-row transactions, the date and payment type only appear on the first row. Row 3 (the continuation of the transaction starting in Row 2) has empty date and payment type fields.

After extraction, we apply fill-forward:

fill_forward_fields = ['date','payment_type']

This propagates values down within each transaction:

Before fill-forward:
  Row 2: date=03 Jan, type=CHQ, details=TESCO, out=50
  Row 3: date=—, type=—, details=contd...

After fill-forward:
  Row 2: date=03 Jan, type=CHQ, details=TESCO, out=50
  Row 3: date=03 Jan, type=CHQ, details=contd...  ← Filled in

Why this matters:

Downstream systems expect every transaction to have a date and type. Without fill-forward, Row 3 would have empty date and type, which would cause validation errors or data corruption.

Important: Fill-forward is applied per-page. It doesn't carry across page boundaries. If a transaction spans two pages (rare), you might need to handle it separately.
path: Parsing HSBC Transactions — Handling Multi-Row Transactions & Bookends

items.title: Merge Fields: Combining Multi-Row Text
items.text:
merge_fields = {fields=['details'], separator=' | '}

This combines the details field across rows of the same transaction:

Raw extraction:
  Row 2: details="TESCO CARDIFF"
  Row 3: details="Reference continues"

After merge:
  details="TESCO CARDIFF | Reference continues"

The separator (' | ') joins them. You could use other separators: ' / ', ' — ', '\n', etc. The goal is to preserve all the text while making it clear there are multiple parts.

Why this matters:

Full context is preserved in a single field. When you export to Excel or CSV, each transaction is one row, with details intact.
path: Parsing HSBC Transactions — Handling Multi-Row Transactions & Bookends

items.title: Field Validation & Regex Patterns
items.text:
Each field in the transaction table has a regex pattern:

{field = 'date', column = 0, vital=false, type = "string", string_pattern ='^[0-3][0-9]\s?[A-Z][a-z]{2}\s?[0-3][0-9]$'},

Let's parse this pattern: ^[0-3][0-9]\s?[A-Z][a-z]{2}\s?[0-3][0-9]$

  • ^ — Start of string
  • [0-3][0-9] — 1–31 (day): First digit 0–3, second digit 0–9
  • \s? — Optional space
  • [A-Z][a-z]{2} — 3-letter month: Capital letter followed by 2 lowercase letters (Jan, Feb, Mar, etc.)
  • \s? — Optional space
  • [0-3][0-9] — 1–31 (year abbreviated): 00–31
  • $ — End of string

This matches: "01 Jan 26", "1Jan26", "03 Feb 26", etc. Flexible but strict.

Payment type pattern: (^[A-Z0-9]{1,3}$)|(^[)]{3}$)

This is two alternatives: - Either 1–3 uppercase alphanumeric chars (FPI, CHQ, TRF, DD) — standard payment types - OR three parentheses ")" (a special case for certain HSBC transaction types)

Details pattern: .+

Simple: at least one character. Almost everything matches.

Amount pattern: No regex; it's type = "currency", so it's parsed as a number.

If a field doesn't match its pattern: - vital=true: The entire row is marked as a failure and deleted from output - vital=false: The field is marked as empty, but the row is kept

For HSBC, most fields are vital=false except details. The logic: We can live with missing payment type or amount, but every transaction must have a description.
path: Parsing HSBC Transactions — Handling Multi-Row Transactions & Bookends

items.title: Currency & Numeric Modifiers (Revisited from Post #2)
items.text:
HSBC uses separate columns for paid_out and paid_in:

Transaction Paid Out Paid In Salary received — 2500.00 ATM withdrawal 100.00 — Transfer out 50.00 —

Both are stored as positive values in the PDF. Downstream systems typically expect a single amount column with sign: - Received £2500 → amount = +2500 - Spent £100 → amount = -100

HSBC doesn't use numeric_modifier on paid_in or paid_out (they're already positive/negative contextually). But the balance column uses it:

{field = '£_balance', column = 5, vital=false, type = "currency", numeric_modifier = {suffix = "D", multiplier = -1.0000}},

Same logic as Post #2: If balance ends with "D", it's inverted (multiply by -1).
path: Parsing HSBC Transactions — Handling Multi-Row Transactions & Bookends

items.title: Processing Flags: Row Deletion & Cleanup
items.text:
After extraction, three flags control which rows are kept:

delete_success_false = true
delete_cast_success_false = true
delete_rows_with_missing_vital_fields = true

delete_success_false = true — Remove rows where any field has success=false (extraction failed)

If the date pattern doesn't match (success=false for date field), and this flag is true, the entire row is deleted.

delete_cast_success_false = true — Remove rows where numeric casting failed

If an amount field can't be parsed as a number, the row is deleted.

delete_rows_with_missing_vital_fields = true — Remove rows with any vital field empty

If details is empty (and vital=true), the row is deleted.

These are safety nets: they catch malformed rows before reaching your output. Without them, corrupted data would leak through.
path: Parsing HSBC Transactions — Handling Multi-Row Transactions & Bookends

items.title: Testing Your Transaction Config
items.text:
Here's how to test extraction:

python -m bank_statement_parser import path/to/HSBC_statement.pdf --debug

Expected output: 

Transaction 1: date=01 Jan, type=FPI, details=SALARY EMPLOYER, in=2500, balance=7500
Transaction 2: date=03 Jan, type=CHQ, details=TESCO CARDIFF | Reference, out=50, balance=7450
Transaction 3: date=05 Jan, type=TRF, details=WATER BILL, out=150, balance=7300
...

Common issues and fixes:

Issue Solution "No transactions extracted" Coordinates or vertical_lines are wrong. The parser can't find the table. Use pdfplumber to debug or manually measure PDF. "Date field failing validation" The date format in your PDF doesn't match the regex. Check the actual date format, adjust pattern. "Transactions not merged correctly" Bookend detection logic is wrong. Review start_fields, end_fields, min_non_empty_start/end. Test manually with your PDF. "Details field cut off" string_max_length = 100 might be truncating. Increase if needed (but be careful with very long descriptions). "Extra rows appearing in output" The delete_* flags might be too lenient. Add validation or increase strictness.
path: Parsing HSBC Transactions — Handling Multi-Row Transactions & Bookends

items.title: Handling Variable PDF Layouts
items.text:
One challenge: banks sometimes change their PDF layouts. If HSBC redesigned their transaction table tomorrow, your config would break.

Strategies to handle this:

  1. Multiple bookends: Define multiple bookend rules for different layouts. The parser tries each until one works.
  2. Flexible regex patterns: Use \s+ (flexible whitespace) instead of exact spaces. Use [A-Z0-9]{1,5} instead of hardcoding lengths.
  3. Dynamic column detection: Use allow_text_failover = true to fall back to pdfplumber's automatic column detection if explicit dividers fail.
  4. Versioning: Keep old configs for old PDF versions. When users submit statements, the parser tries new config first, falls back to old if it fails.

HSBC has done {vertical_lines = [...], allow_text_failover = true}, combining explicit boundaries with automatic fallback.
path: Parsing HSBC Transactions — Handling Multi-Row Transactions & Bookends

items.title: Now It's Your Turn: Adapting Multi-Row Transaction Extraction
items.text:
Steps to implement for your bank:

  1. Download a 2–3 page statement to study the transaction table layout
  2. Identify transaction boundaries:
  3. What fields mark a transaction start? (always filled on first row of transaction)
  4. What fields mark a transaction end? (always filled on last row of transaction)
  5. For HSBC, it's payment_type + details for start, amount for end
  6. Find column positions:
  7. Use pdfplumber or manual measurement
  8. Build the vertical_lines array
  9. Define fields with regex patterns:
  10. Date format (how does your bank format dates?)
  11. Payment type or description format
  12. Amount format
  13. Create the transaction table config in statement_tables.toml
  14. Define bookends: Which fields mark start and end of transactions?
  15. Define fill-forward fields: Which fields repeat across rows?
  16. Define merge fields: Which fields need to be combined?
  17. Test with 10–20 transactions: 
    python -m bank_statement_parser import path/to/pdf.pdf --debug
  18. Refine patterns, coordinates, and logic until satisfied

In Post #4, we show how all these configs work together, and how to map raw fields to standardized output.
path: Parsing HSBC Transactions — Handling Multi-Row Transactions & Bookends

items.title: Common Issues & Solutions
items.text:
Q: How do I find the exact pixel coordinates for columns?

A: Use pdfplumber to programmatically extract table structure, or use a PDF viewer that shows coordinates. Trial and error works fine—test, check output, adjust by 10–50 points, re-test. You'll converge quickly.

Q: Why are some transactions being merged when they shouldn't be?

A: Your bookend detection is too loose. Review start_fields and end_fields. Make sure min_non_empty_start and min_non_empty_end are strict enough to distinguish real transaction starts/ends from continuation rows.

Q: What if my bank's transaction table spans multiple pages?

A: Good news: statement_tables.toml has locations without page_number, which means the same location is applied to every page. The parser automatically extracts transactions from all pages and combines them.

Q: Can I extract additional fields (like transaction ID or reference number)?

A: Yes! Add them to the fields array with appropriate column index and regex pattern. The extraction pipeline will handle them like any other field.

items.title: How We Identified HSBC Bank Statements — Building a PDF Detective
items.text: When parsing 100+ bank statements automatically, the first challenge isn't extracting data—it's knowing which bank you're dealing with. We built an HSBC PDF detective using TOML configuration. Here's how we solved it, and how you can do the same for your bank.
path: How We Identified HSBC Bank Statements — Building a PDF Detective

items.title: How We Identified HSBC Bank Statements — Building a PDF Detective
path: How We Identified HSBC Bank Statements — Building a PDF Detective

items.title: Why PDF Bank Detection Matters
items.text:
Imagine you have a folder with 25 PDFs: 12 from HSBC, 6 from NatWest, 3 from Barclays, 2 from TSB, and 2 more from smaller banks. You need to parse them all automatically, extract transactions, and produce a consolidated spreadsheet. But here's the catch: each bank uses a different PDF layout. Your parser can't use the same extraction rules on an HSBC statement that it would use on a NatWest one.

The first step in any bank statement parser is bank identification. Before you extract balances, account numbers, or transactions, you need to answer a simple question: Which bank issued this PDF?

This is where companies.toml comes in. It's the first config file your parser loads, and its job is to scan an unknown PDF and determine its origin. Without it, you're flying blind.
path: How We Identified HSBC Bank Statements — Building a PDF Detective

items.title: The Solution Overview: companies.toml
items.text:
Every bank config starts with a companies.toml file. It's small but crucial—typically 10–15 lines of configuration that tell your parser how to recognize that bank's PDFs.

Here's the high-level flow:

  1. Parser receives an unknown PDF
  2. Opens page 1 and loads all bank identification rules from companies.toml files
  3. For each bank, tries to find a unique piece of identifying text (usually somewhere on page 1)
  4. If the text is found AND matches a regex pattern, the PDF is identified as that bank
  5. Parser stops searching and loads that bank's extraction config
  6. Remaining extraction uses that bank's configuration (accounts, tables, field mappings)

This is Step 1 of the config process. The bank_statement_parser reference guide walks through all 7 steps, but we're focusing on the company identification piece here.

The genius of this approach: identification is fast (milliseconds), and it fails safe. If no bank matches, the user can manually assign one. If multiple banks match (rare), the parser picks the first one and flags it for review.
path: How We Identified HSBC Bank Statements — Building a PDF Detective

items.title: Dissecting HSBC's companies.toml
items.text:
Let's look at what HSBC's bank identifier actually looks like. This is the real config from the openstan project:

[HSBC_UK]
company = 'HSBC Bank UK'
[HSBC_UK.config]
    config = 'Company Info'
    locations = [
        {page_number = 1, top_left = [475,110], bottom_right = [575, 130]},
        {page_number = 1, top_left = [460,145], bottom_right = [575, 165]},
        {page_number = 1, top_left = [460,165], bottom_right = [575, 185]},
    ]
    field = {field = 'website', vital=true, type="string", string_pattern ='^www\.hsbc\.co\.uk$'}

Let's break down each part:

[HSBC_UK] — This is the unique identifier for the HSBC_UK company config. It must be unique across all banks in your project (you can't have two entries with the same name). This identifier is used later when you define account types.

company = 'HSBC Bank UK' — A human-readable name. This isn't used for detection; it's just for logging and output. When the parser successfully identifies a statement, it records this name so you know which bank it came from.

config = 'Company Info' — A label for this extraction step. During parsing, the system logs each step it tries: "Attempting Company Info extraction on HSBC_UK..." This is purely for debugging. If extraction fails, you'll see which step failed.

locations array — This is where the magic happens. It's an array of rectangular regions (bounding boxes) on page 1 of the PDF. Each location has: - page_number = 1 — Always page 1 for company detection (we're identifying the bank, not individual accounts) - top_left = [475,110] — Top-left corner of the rectangle: x=475, y=110 (in PDF points, not pixels—important distinction!) - bottom_right = [575, 130] — Bottom-right corner: x=575, y=130

These coordinates define a small rectangular region on the PDF. The parser will crop to this region and look for text.

field = {...} — This defines what to extract and how to validate it: - field = 'website' — The name of the field we're extracting (mostly for internal use) - vital=true — This field is mandatory. If extraction fails, the entire company detection fails - type="string" — We're extracting text (not a number or currency) - string_pattern ='^www\.hsbc\.co\.uk$' — The extracted text must match this regex pattern exactly

That regex pattern is strict: ^www\.hsbc\.co\.uk$ means: - ^ — start of string - www\.hsbc\.co\.uk — literal text "www.hsbc.co.uk" (the backslashes escape the dots so they're literal, not wildcards) - $ — end of string

So it matches "www.hsbc.co.uk" and nothing else. No "HSBC Investment", no "m.hsbc.co.uk", no leading/trailing whitespace. Perfect.
path: How We Identified HSBC Bank Statements — Building a PDF Detective

items.title: Why Three Locations? (Lessons from Real Statements)
items.text:
Here's something you'll discover when parsing real-world bank statements: nothing is perfectly consistent.

Different HSBC PDFs might have the website URL in slightly different positions depending on: - Which HSBC product you're using (current account, savings, credit card) - Whether it's a joint account (different formatting) - When the statement was generated (banks redesign PDFs occasionally)

So instead of relying on a single coordinate, the HSBC config has three locations. The parser tries them in order:

  1. Try location 1: crop to [475,110] → [575,130], search for text
  2. If text found AND matches regex → Success! Bank identified.
  3. If not found or doesn't match → continue to location 2
  4. Try location 2: crop to [460,145] → [575,165], search for text
  5. If text found AND matches regex → Success!
  6. If not → continue to location 3
  7. Try location 3: crop to [460,165] → [575,185], search for text
  8. If text found AND matches regex → Success!
  9. If not → Bank detection fails (try next bank's config)

This fallback strategy means the parser can handle slight variations in PDF layout. If HSBC redesigns their statements and the website URL moves 50 pixels down, we update one or two location coordinates instead of rewriting the entire config.
path: How We Identified HSBC Bank Statements — Building a PDF Detective

items.title: Regex Patterns: From Loose to Strict
items.text:
The website URL pattern is just one example. Let's talk about pattern matching in general, because this is where false positives can creep in.

Imagine you wanted a loose regex: .*hsbc.*

This would match: - ✓ "www.hsbc.co.uk" - ✓ "HSBC Bank UK" - ✓ "HSBC Investment Management" - ✓ "Contact HSBC here"

Too loose! You'd accidentally identify non-HSBC PDFs containing the word "HSBC".

A tighter regex: hsbc\.co\.uk

Better, but still risky: - ✓ "www.hsbc.co.uk" - ✓ "https://hsbc.co.uk" - ✓ "api.hsbc.co.uk" - ✓ "m.hsbc.co.uk"

The last two aren't what we want. Mobile and API domains are unlikely to appear on a retail statement.

The strict regex HSBC uses: ^www\.hsbc\.co\.uk$

Perfect: - ✓ "www.hsbc.co.uk" - ✗ "https://www.hsbc.co.uk" (extra text at start) - ✗ "www.hsbc.co.uk/en" (extra text at end) - ✗ "api.hsbc.co.uk" (different domain)

This level of specificity is crucial. You want high confidence that you've identified the right bank before proceeding with extraction rules designed specifically for that bank.

Quick regex cheatsheet for bank configs:

Pattern Matches ^text$ Exact match (nothing before or after) ^text Starts with text text$ Ends with text \. Literal dot (backslash escapes it) [A-Z0-9]+ One or more uppercase letters or digits \d{2}-\d{2}-\d{2} Exactly 2-2-2 digits (e.g., sort code) \| Literal pipe character (backslash escapes it)
path: How We Identified HSBC Bank Statements — Building a PDF Detective

items.title: The Extraction Pipeline: What Happens When the Parser Sees a New PDF
items.text:
Let's trace through the entire company detection process step-by-step:

  1. User loads a PDF into the parser (e.g., their HSBC statement from January)
  2. Parser opens page 1 and extracts text
  3. Parser loads the config — It reads companies.toml for all supported banks (HSBC_UK, NatWest_UK, TSB_UK, Barclays_UK, etc.)
  4. For each bank, it tries each location in order:
  5. HSBC_UK, location 1: crop PDF to [475,110] → [575,130]
    • Text found: "www.hsbc.co.uk"
    • Regex check: Does "www.hsbc.co.uk" match ^www\.hsbc\.co\.uk$? YES ✓
    • PDF identified as HSBC_UK. Stop searching.
  6. Parser loads HSBC-specific config (accounts.toml, statement_types.toml, etc.)
  7. Continue with account identification, balance extraction, transaction extraction (covered in Posts #2 and #3)

If location 1 had failed (no text found, or text didn't match the regex), the parser would have tried locations 2 and 3 before giving up on HSBC. Only after all HSBC locations are exhausted would it try the next bank's config.

This entire process takes milliseconds. Even with 20+ banks in your config, PDF identification is lightning-fast.
path: How We Identified HSBC Bank Statements — Building a PDF Detective

items.title: Common Issues & Troubleshooting
items.text:
Q: My HSBC statement isn't being detected. What went wrong?

A: The coordinates are probably wrong. HSBC might have redesigned their PDFs, or your statement version is different. - Open your PDF in a PDF reader - Manually locate the "www.hsbc.co.uk" text - Note its approximate position on the page (you can use the PDF viewer's pointer) - Adjust the coordinates and try again - Or add a 4th location to the config (more fallback options = better coverage)

Q: Why use PDF points instead of pixel coordinates?

A: PDF points are a standard measurement (1/72 inch) built into the PDF format. They're consistent across different viewers and screen resolutions. Pixels are screen-dependent and unreliable for PDF extraction.

Q: How many locations do I need?

A: Start with 1–2. If that covers 90% of statements from that bank, you're good. If you encounter variations, add more locations. HSBC uses 3; most banks can do with 2–3. Beyond 5 locations, it's usually better to change your identifying text (find something more consistent).

Q: Can I use multiple identifying texts (not just the website)?

A: Yes! You could identify HSBC by its website URL, or by its logo, or by specific header text. If the logo changes positions frequently, you might add another location that looks for a text header instead. Mix-and-match whatever's most reliable for that bank.
path: How We Identified HSBC Bank Statements — Building a PDF Detective

items.title: Extending This to Other HSBC Account Types
items.text:
One thing worth mentioning: this companies.toml works for HSBC Current Accounts, Savings Accounts, Credit Cards, and ISAs. They all have "www.hsbc.co.uk" in roughly the same location on page 1.

The account-type-specific config happens later—in accounts.toml (covered in Post #2). Company detection is bank-level; account detection is product-level. This separation of concerns means less duplication and easier maintenance.

items.title: Now It's Your Turn: Building a PDF Detector for Your Bank
items.text:
Ready to try this for your own bank? Here's the process:

  1. Download a few PDFs from your bank. (3–5 statements, preferably from different months)
  2. Open one in a PDF viewer and examine page 1.
  3. Find a unique identifying piece of text:
  4. Bank website (most reliable)
  5. Bank name or logo (if consistent)
  6. Specific header text unique to that bank
  7. Account type label
  8. Note its approximate location on the page (you're looking for rough coordinates; exact pixel-perfect precision isn't required, we'll refine later).
  9. Write a regex pattern that matches that text (and nothing else).
  10. Create your first companies.toml entry in a new folder: project/config/import/YOUR_BANK_COUNTRY/companies.toml
  11. Test with 3–5 statements: 
    python -m bank_statement_parser identify path/to/pdf.pdf
  12. If detection works: congratulations! Move on to account type detection (Post #2). If detection fails: adjust coordinates or regex pattern and retry.

The bank_statement_parser contributing guide has more detail if you get stuck.
path: How We Identified HSBC Bank Statements — Building a PDF Detective

items.title: Additional FAQs
items.text:
Q: What's the difference between top_left and bottom_right?

A: They define a rectangular bounding box. top_left = [475,110] is the top-left corner (x=475, y=110). bottom_right = [575, 130] is the bottom-right corner. The parser crops the PDF to this rectangle and searches for text inside. Make sure you're measuring on the right page and accounting for where text actually appears.

Q: Can I use multiple companies.toml files?

A: No, companies.toml must be a single file per bank folder. But you can have multiple banks configured. Each bank gets its own folder (HSBC_UK, NatWest_UK, etc.) with its own companies.toml.

Q: What if my bank's identifying text changes between statement versions?

A: Add more locations. If location 1 looks for the website URL and location 2 looks for a logo, you've covered both old and new formats. The parser will try locations in order until one succeeds.

items.title: How to Export Multiple Bank Accounts to One Excel File
items.text:
You've got statements from three different banks sitting in your downloads folder. Your self-assessment deadline is approaching, or maybe you're sorting out someone's estate and the solicitor needs everything in one spreadsheet. Copying rows by hand from each PDF is the kind of task that chews up a whole evening and still feels uncertain when you're done.

There's a calmer way. openstan lets you import all your PDFs at once, then export bank statements to Excel in a single file — sorted, labelled by account, no manual copying required.

items.title: Why this is harder than it looks
items.text:
Bank PDFs are not designed to talk to each other. HSBC formats its dates one way; NatWest uses a different layout entirely; TSB might split credits and debits into separate columns. If you've ever tried to copy-paste three months of transactions into a single spreadsheet and then discovered a column mismatch on row 47, you'll know exactly what that costs you in time and trust.

The goal here isn't just to export — it's to end up with a single, clean table where every row is correctly attributed to the right account and every date is in the same format. That's what makes the file actually useful to an accountant, a probate solicitor, or HMRC.
path: How to Export Multiple Bank Accounts to One Excel File

items.title: What you'll need before you start
items.text:
• Your statement PDFs, downloaded from each bank's online portal. Most UK banks let you download up to seven years.
  • openstan installed on your computer — there's a native installer for Windows, macOS, and Linux; no Python required.
  • About five minutes.

You don't need to rename or reorganise anything. openstan extracts the bank name and account type from inside each PDF during processing, then saves its own renamed copies into the project's statements folder. Your original files stay untouched, wherever they are.

So you can point openstan at a folder — or several folders — of statements with their original downloaded filenames and it just works. If the same statement appears twice (an easy thing to do when you're gathering from multiple sources), duplicates are harmless: openstan quietly ignores them. And if a statement is missing, it flags the gap for you rather than leaving you to wonder why the numbers don't add up.

statements/
├── HSBC_CurrentAccount_Oct2024.pdf
├── HSBC_CurrentAccount_Nov2024.pdf
├── NatWest_Current_Oct2024.pdf
└── TSB_Savings_Oct2024.pdf

Messy real-world filenames, all in one folder — that's fine.
path: How to Export Multiple Bank Accounts to One Excel File

items.title: Step 1 — Create a project
items.text:
Open openstan and click New Project. Give it a name that means something later ("2024–25 Tax Year" or "Estate of J. Smith"), then choose a folder to save the project database. Click Create. This is where openstan will store the project database and its renamed copies of your statements — keep it somewhere you'll find again.

If you've not done this before, the Quick Start guide walks through the first project in about five minutes.
path: How to Export Multiple Bank Accounts to One Excel File

items.title: Step 2 — Import all your statements at once
items.text:
Click Import Statements. You can select individual PDFs, or select an entire folder and let openstan work through it. Hold Shift or Ctrl to select multiple files at once.

openstan reads the account name, sort code, and transaction data directly from each PDF. You don't need to tell it which bank you're using — it detects that automatically from the file contents. Twelve months of statements from three banks typically processes in under a minute.

Once the import preview appears, you'll see:

  • Each account listed separately, with the bank name openstan detected
  • A count of transactions per statement
  • Any duplicate warnings — useful if the same period overlaps across two downloads
  • Balance verification — openstan checks that opening and closing balances match between consecutive statements

When everything looks right, click Commit. See the Import Results screen guide for a full walkthrough of what each flag means.
path: How to Export Multiple Bank Accounts to One Excel File

items.title: Step 3 — Export to Excel
items.text:
Click Export Data (or press Alt+E). The Export Data panel gives you three choices for format — Excel, CSV, or JSON — and two choices for type:

Type What it produces Single One flat table: every transaction from every account, with an "Account" column to tell them apart. Best for accountants and spreadsheet work. Multi Separate tables for accounts, statements, transactions, balances, and gaps. Best for loading into a database or BI tool.

For most purposes — self-assessment, probate, or a quick review with your accountant — Single + Excel is the right combination. Choose your export folder, click Export Excel, and you're done.

The resulting file looks something like this:

Date Account Description Debit Credit Balance 2024-10-01 HSBC Current Opening Balance — 3,200.00 3,200.00 2024-10-03 HSBC Current SALARY EMPLOYER LTD — 2,800.00 6,000.00 2024-10-07 NatWest Current DIRECT DEBIT UTILITIES 87.50 — 1,412.50 2024-10-12 TSB Savings TRANSFER IN — 400.00 2,900.00

Every date is in ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DD), regardless of how each bank originally presented it.

For details on all the export options, see the Export Data screen guide.
path: How to Export Multiple Bank Accounts to One Excel File

items.title: Who this helps most
items.text:
The Self Assessment use case is the most common reason people reach for this workflow. You've got twelve months of PDFs from your current account — perhaps a savings account too — and your accountant needs a flat file they can sort and filter. Doing it manually is genuinely risky: a missed row or a misread decimal is the sort of thing that causes an amendment down the line.

If you're managing an estate, the Probate & Estate Admin use case covers some additional considerations — particularly around gathering statements from multiple banks when you're acting as executor.

And if you run a small business with separate personal and business accounts, the Multi-Account Tracking use case explains how to keep those clearly separated inside the same project.
path: How to Export Multiple Bank Accounts to One Excel File

items.title: What usually trips people up
items.text:
"openstan didn't detect my bank correctly." A handful of PDFs — especially older ones or those downloaded via a mobile app rather than online banking — can vary in layout. If a statement imports with no transactions, try downloading the same period again from your bank's desktop website. The Supported Bank Accounts lists the currently supported formats.

"Some months are missing." openstan flags gaps automatically after you commit. If it shows a gap between November and January, that's your cue to download the missing December statement. You don't have to guess — the gap detection does that check for you.

"The balances don't match between two statements." This usually means two overlapping downloads (e.g., a year-end summary PDF that duplicates transactions from monthly statements). openstan will warn you about duplicates in the import preview. Remove the overlapping file and re-import.
path: How to Export Multiple Bank Accounts to One Excel File

items.title: FAQ
items.text:
Do I need to import each bank separately? No. You can select PDFs from every bank in a single import batch. openstan reads the account details from each file and keeps them separate in the database. Everything lands in one project, ready to export together.

Will the export work for HMRC? The Excel format openstan produces is a plain .xlsx file — the same format accountants and tax agents work with every day. HMRC doesn't mandate a specific format for records you keep yourself; what matters is that the data is accurate and complete. For guidance on what HMRC actually expects, GOV.UK's self-assessment record-keeping page is the authoritative source.

Can I filter the export to just one account or one date range? The Standard Exports tab exports all committed data. For filtered or custom exports — say, just the current account between April and April — see the Advanced Export screen, which uses TOML configuration files to define precisely what gets included. Alternatively, you can build your own reports for export, specifying columns and filters - see the Run Reports section of the documentation.

What if I only have CSV downloads, not PDFs? openstan's primary input is PDF bank statements. If your bank provides CSV exports, those are typically already spreadsheet-ready — you may be able to combine them directly in Excel. That said, if you want gap detection, balance verification, and a clean combined view, importing PDFs via openstan is worth the extra step of downloading them from your bank's portal.

Is my data uploaded anywhere? No. openstan processes everything locally on your machine. Nothing is sent to any server. See the Privacy Policy for the formal version, but the short answer is: your statements never leave your computer.

items.title: Admin
items.text: The Admin dialog is used for project management operations that modify or remove data. It is intentionally hidden from the main navigation to prevent accidental use.

items.title: Opening the Admin dialog
items.text: Click the Admin button in the top-right corner of the application title bar. A confirmation is not required to open the dialog — destructive actions inside the dialog each have their own confirmation step.

items.title: Delete Project
items.text:
Permanently removes a project from both the openstan UI database and, optionally, from disk.

Control Description Project drop-down Select the project to delete. Also delete the project folder from disk checkbox When ticked, the project folder and all its contents are deleted from the filesystem after the UI record is removed. Delete Project button Initiates deletion after a confirmation dialog.

This cannot be undone

If Also delete the project folder from disk is ticked, all statement PDFs, configuration files, and the project database are permanently deleted. Ensure you have a backup before proceeding.

items.title: Remove Project from UI Only
items.text:
Removes a project from the openstan application database without touching any files on disk. The project folder remains intact and can be re-added later using Add Existing Project.

Control Description Project drop-down Select the project to remove. Remove from UI button Removes the project registration after a confirmation dialog.

Use this option if you want to temporarily hide a project from the selector, or if you are moving a project folder and will re-register it from its new location.

items.title: Reset Application
items.text:
Deletes and recreates the openstan application database (gui.db), effectively returning the application to a clean first-run state.

All project registrations are removed. Project folders on disk are not affected.

Click Empty Database & Restart to proceed. A confirmation dialog is shown before any action is taken. The application closes and must be restarted manually after the reset completes.

Use with care

After a reset, all projects must be re-added via Add Existing Project. The project data (statements, transactions) stored in each project folder is unaffected.

items.title: Anonymise PDF
items.text:
Opens the Anonymise PDF tool for the currently active project.

Control Description Open Anonymise Tool button Opens the Anonymise PDF dialog, where you can select a PDF or folder, edit the exclusion config, and produce anonymised copies.

Use this to create anonymised versions of PDFs that are safe to share or attach to a GitHub issue. The tool supports both single-file and folder batch processing. It is also accessible directly from the nav bar (primary entry point) or from any REVIEW or FAILURE row in the Debug Info dialog.

A project must be active

The button is only useful when a project is open. If no project is selected, an error dialog is shown.

items.title: View Logs
items.text:
The View Logs section provides access to application and project log files for troubleshooting and diagnostics.

Control Description View Application Log button Opens the log viewer displaying application-wide events and diagnostics from the current session. Shows startup information, menu actions, and general errors. Always enabled. View Project Log button Opens the log viewer displaying project-specific operations, statement imports, parser diagnostics, and anonymisation details. Only enabled when a project is selected.

For detailed information about logs, including how to find log files manually and how to share logs with support, see the Logging & Debugging Guide.

items.title: Logging Settings
items.text:
The Logging Settings section controls diagnostic verbosity levels across the application and dependent libraries.

Control Description Enable verbose mode checkbox When checked, enables DEBUG-level logging (shows detailed per-field extraction, database operations, and library diagnostics from bank_statement_parser and uk_bank_statement_anonymiser). Useful for troubleshooting and when reporting issues to support. Changes apply immediately without restarting the app. Help icon (question mark) Hover to see a tooltip explaining verbose mode and when to use it.

For more information, see the Enabling Verbose Mode section of the Logging guide.

items.title: Advanced Export
items.text: The Advanced Export tab lives inside the Export Data panel (Alt+E). It provides spec-driven custom exports where you control the account, statement, and date range, and the output format is defined by a TOML export spec file.

items.title: Account
items.text: A drop-down listing all accounts in the project. The first option, \<all accounts>, runs the export across every account.

items.title: Statement
items.text: A drop-down that updates automatically when you change the Account selection. Lists all statements for the selected account, plus (all statements) as the first option.

items.title: Date from / Date to
items.text:
Date range filters. By default, both are disabled (the All dates checkbox is ticked), meaning no date filtering is applied.

  • Untick All dates to enable the date picker and set a specific start or end date.
  • You can set one or both limits independently.

items.title: Export specs
items.text:
The lower section of the panel lists the available export specs for the active project.

Each spec is a .toml file located in the project's config/export/ directory. For each spec found, a button is shown displaying:

  • The spec's description (from inside the TOML file).
  • The spec's filename in smaller text below.

Click a button to run that spec with the current parameter selections. A progress bar and status label show the export progress.

If the config/export/ directory contains no .toml files, the panel shows:

No export specs found

items.title: Creating and modifying export spec TOML files
items.text:
Export specs are TOML configuration files that define the shape and content of a custom export. For a full guide to creating and editing these files, see the bank_statement_parser export documentation.

Where to put spec files

Place your .toml export spec files in <project-folder>/config/export/. openstan rescans this directory each time you open the Export Data panel.

items.title: Anonymise PDF
items.text: The Anonymise PDF tool lets you produce redacted copies of bank statement PDFs suitable for sharing — for example, when attaching a failing statement to a GitHub issue. You can anonymise a single file or an entire folder of PDFs in one go. All text is scrambled by default. You use two simple tables to control which phrases are left unchanged (so the parser can still read them) and which strings are replaced with safe alternatives (before scrambling occurs). An optional retain descriptions mode lets you skip the scrambling pass for transaction descriptions, applying only your explicit always-anonymise replacements and numeric ID substitutions.

items.title: Opening the tool
items.text:
The Anonymise tool can be opened from three places:

  • Nav bar → Anonymise Statements button (Alt+A) — the primary entry point.
  • Admin dialog → Anonymise PDF section → Open Anonymise Tool button.
  • Debug Info dialog → Anonymise button on any REVIEW or FAILURE row — the tool opens pre-loaded with that statement's PDF path.

items.title: Selecting a source PDF
items.text:
You can anonymise files one at a time or process an entire folder at once:

  • Browse… — opens a file picker to select a single PDF.
  • Browse Folder… — opens a folder picker. openstan recursively discovers all .pdf files in the selected folder and its subdirectories. A count of discovered files is shown below the path field.

If the tool was opened from the Debug Info dialog, the path is pre-filled with the failing statement's path (single-file mode).

items.title: Configuring Anonymisation
items.text: The center panel contains two tabs for managing anonymisation rules. Configurations are saved automatically when you run the anonymisation or close the dialog (with retry logic if the first save attempt fails).

items.title: Always Anonymise Tab
items.text:
Entries in this table force exact string replacements before the scrambling pass. Use this for structured data like sort codes or account numbers you want to replace with safe placeholders.

  • Original Text column: the string to find (case-sensitive)
  • Replacement column: the string to substitute
  • Click Add Row to add a new replacement pair
  • Click Remove Selected to delete a row

Example:

Original Text Replacement 11-22-33 00-00-00 12345678 00000000 ACME Bank Bank

items.title: Never Anonymise Tab
items.text:
Phrases listed here are excluded from scrambling. Use this for structural text the parser needs to read (e.g., column headers, balance labels, transaction type codes).

  • Phrase column: text to leave unchanged (matching is case-insensitive)
  • Click Add Row to add a new phrase
  • Click Remove Selected to delete a row

Example:

Phrase Balance Brought Forward Date Money In Money Out

Iterating

The typical workflow is: run → open both PDFs → notice what structural text is unreadable → add those phrases to the Never Anonymise tab → run again. Repeat until the anonymised PDF is both sufficiently redacted and parseable.

items.title: Running the anonymisation
items.text:
Click Run Anonymisation.

Single-file mode: The tool calls bsa.anonymise_pdf in a background thread so the UI remains responsive. The anonymised PDF is written alongside the source file with anonymised_ prepended to the filename (after any filename replacements are applied).

Folder mode: A confirmation dialog warns that each file must be reviewed individually before sharing — automated anonymisation may not catch all sensitive information. Once confirmed, a progress bar shows "Anonymising file N of M…" as each PDF is processed. All output files are written to an anonymised/ subfolder inside the selected folder.

When the batch completes, the status line shows the number of files that succeeded or failed.

Re-running overwrites the previous output

Each run writes to the same output path. If you need to preserve a previous version, move or rename it before running again.

items.title: Retaining transaction descriptions
items.text: By default, all text in the PDF is scrambled — including transaction descriptions. An optional Retain transaction descriptions checkbox in the Run Anonymisation section lets you skip the scrambling pass, applying only your explicit Always Anonymise replacements and numeric ID substitutions (sort codes, account numbers, card numbers). Transaction descriptions and free text are left unchanged.

items.title: When to use this
items.text: This option is useful when you need to demonstrate or test the parser's output with realistic-looking transaction descriptions — for example, in aggregated reports or internal demos where readability matters more than full redaction.

items.title: How it works
items.text:
1. The checkbox only appears when your Always Anonymise table contains at least one non-empty replacement row. This is a hard requirement — the underlying library raises an error if no always-anonymise file is provided, because sensitive names and addresses would otherwise remain un-anonymised.
  2. Checking the box triggers a security warning dialog. You must confirm that you understand the risks before the option is enabled.
  3. When active, the status label shows [Retain descriptions: ON] so you can see at a glance that descriptions will not be scrambled.
  4. The checkbox resets each time you open the dialog — you must re-confirm the warning on every session.

Security warning

Enabling this option means transaction descriptions and free text are not scrambled. Transaction descriptions may contain personally identifiable information such as merchant names, payment references, or addresses.

  • Ensure you have added all personally identifiable information to your Always Anonymise file before using this option.
  • Files produced with retain descriptions enabled must not be shared externally. Use them only for internal testing and demonstration at an aggregated level.

items.title: Viewing the results
items.text:
Single-file mode: Once a run completes, Open Original PDF and Open Anonymised PDF both become active. Click either button to open the file in your system's default PDF viewer. Open both to compare them side-by-side.

Button Action Open Original PDF Opens the source PDF in the system viewer. Available as soon as a file is selected. Open Anonymised PDF Opens the anonymised output in the system viewer. Enabled after a successful run.

Folder mode: After the batch completes, two additional buttons appear:

Button Action View Anonymised Files… Opens a results table showing the status, original path, and anonymised path for every file. Each row has Original and Anonymised buttons to open the corresponding file. Open Output Folder Opens the anonymised/ subfolder in your operating system's file manager.

items.title: Config File Locations
items.text:
The app stores two TOML files in:

<project folder>/config/user/
  • always_anonymise.toml — forced replacements (original → replacement pairs)
  • never_anonymise.toml — phrases excluded from scrambling

Both files are created automatically when the project is first initialised or connected. You can also edit them directly outside of openstan with any text editor (TOML format). Changes made outside the app are loaded the next time you open the Anonymise tool.

Keep config files out of source control

These files may contain substrings of real sort codes or account numbers used as matching patterns. Treat them as sensitive and exclude them from any repository you share.

items.text: The Export Data panel (Alt+E) lets you export your committed transaction data to Excel, CSV, or JSON using configurable presets.

items.title: Placeholder state
items.text: If no statements have been committed yet, the panel shows a placeholder message. Import and commit at least one batch first.

items.title: Export parameters
items.text: Before exporting, configure the following parameters:

items.title: Type
items.text: Option Description Single Exports a single flat transactions table joining all dimensions. Best for spreadsheet analysis. Multi Exports separate star-schema tables: accounts, calendar, statements, transactions, balances, and gaps. Best for loading into an external database or BI tool.

items.title: Batch
items.text:
Option Description All Exports data from all committed batches. Latest Exports data from the most recently committed batch only.

Pending batch detected

If you select Latest and the most recent batch has not yet been committed (i.e. it is still in the results panel), openstan will show a dialog asking whether to export the last committed batch or return to review the pending one.

items.title: File naming
items.text: Option Description Timestamp files Each export run creates new files with a timestamp in the filename (e.g. transactions_20240115_143022.xlsx). Previous exports are preserved. Overwrite Each export run overwrites the previous files with the same fixed filename.

items.title: Export folder
items.text:
The folder where exported files will be saved. Defaults to an exports/ subfolder inside the project directory.

  • Click Browse to choose a different folder.
  • Click Reset to restore the default export folder.

items.title: Export format buttons
items.text:
Button Output Export Excel Writes one .xlsx file per table (Single: one file; Multi: one file per table). Export CSV Writes one .csv file per table. Export JSON Writes one .json file per table.

A progress bar is shown while the export is running. A status label confirms completion or reports any errors.

items.title: Import Results
items.text: The Import Results panel appears automatically when a batch finishes processing. It summarises what happened and lets you decide what to do next.

items.title: Summary bar
items.text:
A single line at the top of the panel shows counts for the current batch:

Counter Meaning Total Total number of PDF files submitted. Pending Files not yet processed (only visible during a running import). Processed Files for which processing has completed (success or failure). Success Files parsed cleanly with matching checks and balances. Review Files parsed but with checks-and-balances discrepancies. Failed Files that could not be parsed.

items.title: Result tabs
items.text: Results are split across three tabs. Each tab is hidden if it has no rows.

items.title: SUCCESS tab
items.text:
Lists all statements that were parsed cleanly. Columns typically include the filename, detected bank, account details, statement date range, and transaction count.

Statements in this tab will be written to the project database when you click Commit Batch.

items.title: REVIEW tab
items.text:
Lists statements where parsing succeeded but the extracted opening/closing balances do not reconcile with the sum of transactions. This often indicates a parsing issue with a specific statement format variant.

These statements are not committed even if you click Commit Batch. Investigate them using View Debug Info before deciding whether to proceed.

items.title: FAILURE tab
items.text:
Lists statements that could not be parsed at all. Common causes:

  • The bank is not supported (no TOML configuration exists).
  • The PDF is password-protected, corrupted, or not a real bank statement.
  • A new statement format has been introduced by the bank that differs from the configured layout.

items.title: Debug Info dialog
items.text:
Click View Debug Info to open a dialog showing per-file debug output for all REVIEW and FAILURE statements.

Column Description Statement The PDF filename. Type REVIEW or FAILURE. Debug Status Processing state: pending → running → done / error / unavailable. Open JSON Opens the debug JSON output file in your system's default JSON viewer (enabled once the file is generated). Open PDF Opens the original PDF in your system's default PDF viewer. Anonymise Opens the Anonymise PDF tool pre-loaded with this statement's path, so you can produce a redacted copy to attach to a GitHub issue. Message The error or review message from the parser.

A progress indicator at the bottom of the dialog shows how many debug files have been generated.

Getting help with a failing statement

If a statement fails or produces unexpected results, the Anonymise button pre-loads the failing file into the Anonymise PDF tool so you can produce a safe, redacted copy to share.

  • Existing supported bank — unexpected result: open a parsing issue on the bank_statement_parser repo and attach the anonymised statement.
  • Bank not yet supported: open a new bank request or follow the Adding a new bank guide if you'd like to configure it yourself.

items.title: Action buttons
items.text:
Button Action Close Results Returns to the Import Statements queue panel. The batch remains open — you can return to results at any time via View Statement Results. Abandon Batch Discards all results for this batch and unlocks the import queue. This cannot be undone. View Debug Info Opens the Debug Info dialog (enabled when REVIEW or FAILURE rows exist). Commit Batch Writes all SUCCESS-status statements to the project database and closes the batch. Enabled only when at least one SUCCESS row exists.

REVIEW statements are not committed

Clicking Commit Batch commits only SUCCESS statements. REVIEW statements remain unimported. If you want to investigate and re-import a REVIEW statement, use Abandon Batch, fix the issue, and re-run the import.

After committing

Once a batch is committed, the Project Info, Export Data, and Run Reports navigation items become visible (or are updated if they were already visible).

items.title: Import Statements
items.text: The Import Statements panel (Alt+I) is where you build a queue of bank statement PDFs and run the import process.

items.title: Building the import queue
items.text: The queue is displayed as a tree. Folders appear as collapsible parent nodes; individual PDF files appear as children.

items.title: Adding files
items.text:
Button Action Add Folders of Statements Opens a folder browser. All PDF files found directly inside the selected folder are added as a group. Add Individual Statement Files Opens a multi-select file picker. Choose one or more PDF files to add.

You can add files from multiple different folders in a single queue — each folder becomes a separate group in the tree.

items.title: Removing files
items.text:
Button Action Remove Selected Removes the files currently highlighted in the tree. Select a folder node to remove all files in that group. Enabled only when at least one item is selected. Clear All Statements Removes every item from the queue. Enabled only when the queue is non-empty.

Duplicate detection

Attempting to add a file that is already in the queue has no effect — duplicates are silently ignored.

items.title: Running the import
items.text:
Click Run Statement Import (bottom right) to start processing. This button is disabled until the queue contains at least one file.

During processing:

  • A lock status label appears indicating the batch is in progress.
  • The queue controls are disabled — no files can be added or removed while a batch is running.
  • Control returns to the Import Results panel automatically when processing completes.

Do not close the application during import

Closing openstan while an import is running will leave the batch in an incomplete state. If this happens, use Abandon Batch in the results panel on next launch to reset the queue.

Diagnosing import failures

If statements land in the REVIEW or FAILURE tabs, enable verbose mode and re-run the import for detailed per-field diagnostics. See the Logging & Debugging Guide for instructions.

items.title: Reviewing a pending batch
items.text: If a previous import run has not yet been committed or abandoned, a View Statement Results button appears at the bottom left of the panel. Click it to return to the Import Results panel for that batch.

items.title: Supported file types
items.text: openstan processes PDF files only. Other file types in the selected folders are ignored.

items.title: Bank support
items.text:
Parsing is handled by the bank_statement_parser library. A parser configuration (a set of TOML files) must exist for each bank whose statements you want to import.

If your bank is not yet supported, refer to the bank_statement_parser guide on adding a new bank for instructions on creating and modifying the TOML configuration files.
